entries.meaning: Look into something and deal with it — and, said flatly, refuse it.
examples: I need to see about a new passport before we travel.
She went inside to see about getting us a table.
Could you see about the leak in the basement?
He says he's dropping out? We'll see about that.
You think you can park in my spot? We'll see about it.

senses.head: Attend to something, look into it
body: The everyday sense: take charge of a job that still needs doing. Close to see to, but see about leans toward finding out what is involved, while see to is getting it finished. (заняться, разобраться с)
examples: I need to see about a new passport before we travel.
She went inside to see about getting us a table.
Could you see about the leak in the basement?

senses.head: we'll see about that — a flat refusal
body: With the stress on that, it announces that the speaker intends to stop whatever was just said. (ну это мы ещё посмотрим)
examples: He says he's dropping out? We'll see about that.
You think you can park in my spot? We'll see about it.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: see about the tickets, see about it. ✗ see the tickets about.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — a noun, an -ing form, or it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; attending to something is a task you perform, and it takes the progressive freely: she's seeing about a table for us. Sense 2 (we'll see about that) is a fixed formula, not a free verb.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic here: ✗ a new passport was seen about, ✗ the leak has been seen about. Use see to when you need a passive.
entries.see also: see to, see through, set about

entries.meaning: Go with someone to the airport, station, or door to say goodbye — or drive an opponent away.
examples: We got up at four to see her off at the airport.
The whole town came to see off the recruits.
Don't bother seeing me off — I'll grab a cab.
The dog saw off two coyotes before dawn.
They saw the challengers off in straight sets.
He saw them off with nothing but a flashlight and a lot of yelling.

senses.head: Say goodbye at the point of departure
body: You travel part of the way with the person purely in order to wave. (провожать)
examples: We got up at four to see her off at the airport.
The whole town came to see off the recruits.
Don't bother seeing me off — I'll grab a cab.

senses.head: Drive away, fend off
body: Of a rival, an intruder, or a challenge; very common in sports writing. (отбить, дать отпор)
examples: The dog saw off two coyotes before dawn.
They saw the challengers off in straight sets.
He saw them off with nothing but a flashlight and a lot of yelling.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: проводить (на вокзал, в аэропорт); отбить, дать отпор
entries.separable: yes — see off the visitors or see the visitors off, and with a pronoun it must split: see them off, never ✗ see off them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: going to the gate to wave, and driving a rival away.
entries.passive: yes in both senses — the recruits were seen off by the whole town; the challengers were seen off in straight sets.
entries.see also: see out, send off, show out

entries.meaning: Stay with something until it ends, or walk a guest to the door.
examples: She plans to see out her contract and then move to Denver.
He saw the winter out in a cabin with no phone.
It's a bad season, but we'll see it out.
The assistant saw the visitors out through the side entrance.
Please don't get up — I'll see myself out.

senses.head: Last until the end of a period
body: Of a contract, a term, a season, a winter — you stay in place until the clock runs out. (продержаться до конца, доработать)
examples: She plans to see out her contract and then move to Denver.
He saw the winter out in a cabin with no phone.
It's a bad season, but we'll see it out.

senses.head: Escort someone to the door
body: A shade politer than show out; the reflexive see myself out is the standard way to leave without being walked. (проводить до двери)
examples: The assistant saw the visitors out through the side entrance.
Please don't get up — I'll see myself out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: доработать до конца, продержаться до конца; проводить до двери
entries.separable: yes — see out the year or see the year out; with a pronoun it must split: see it out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is durative (you keep going until the clock runs out), sense 2 a single act of escorting.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in sense 2, the visitors were seen out through the side entrance; strained in sense 1, ✗ her contract was seen out.
entries.see also: see off, see through, show out, sit out

entries.meaning: Carry something to the end, carry someone through a hard stretch, or refuse to be fooled.
examples: Whatever happens, I intend to see this project through.
She saw the reforms through over four long years.
It's a lousy job, but I'll see it through.
Her sense of humor saw her through the divorce.
Two crates of instant noodles saw us through the semester.
His mother saw through the excuse in about a second.
Voters see right through that kind of promise.

senses.head: Carry something to the end
body: The object can go on either side, but see it through is the fixed shape most Americans reach for. (довести до конца)
examples: Whatever happens, I intend to see this project through.
She saw the reforms through over four long years.
It's a lousy job, but I'll see it through.

senses.head: Sustain someone through difficulty
body: The subject is whatever keeps the person going, and the person always sits between the verb and the particle. (поддержать, помочь продержаться)
examples: Her sense of humor saw her through the divorce.
Two crates of instant noodles saw us through the semester.

senses.head: Not be fooled by someone
body: Inseparable, and always about a person, a lie, or a performance. (видеть насквозь, раскусить)
examples: His mother saw through the excuse in about a second.
Voters see right through that kind of promise.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: довести до конца; поддержать, помочь продержаться; видеть насквозь
entries.separable: depends on the sense, and this is the entry to get right. Finish it and sustain someone separate, and with a pronoun they must: see it through, her humor saw her through. Not be fooled by never separates: I can see through him — ✗ I can see him through, which would mean something else entirely.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (finishing a job, carrying someone along); sense 3 is a stative verb of perception and resists the progressive: ✗ I'm seeing through him — you say I can see through him.
entries.passive: restricted — good in sense 1, the reforms were seen through over four years, and with a thing in sense 3, the excuse was seen through in about a second. Sense 2 has none: ✗ she was seen through the divorce by her humor.
entries.see also: see out, see off, stick with, stand by

entries.meaning: Take care of something so that it actually gets done.
examples: I'll see to the paperwork if you handle the movers.
The nurse saw to his hand before anyone asked a question.
Who's seeing to the food?
See to it that the doors are locked by ten.
He saw to it that everyone else got paid first.

senses.head: Take care of something
body: Where see about is looking into it, see to is handling it. (позаботиться о, заняться)
examples: I'll see to the paperwork if you handle the movers.
The nurse saw to his hand before anyone asked a question.
Who's seeing to the food?

senses.head: see to it that — make sure
body: A fixed frame with a clause after it. In American English the it is not optional: ✗ see that to. (проследить, чтобы)
examples: See to it that the doors are locked by ten.
He saw to it that everyone else got paid first.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: see to the details, see to it. ✗ see the details to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; handling something to completion, and comfortable in the progressive: who's seeing to the food?
entries.passive: yes — one of the prepositional verbs that passivizes cleanly: his hand was seen to before anyone asked a question, has the paperwork been seen to? The frame see to it that has no passive.
entries.see also: see about, set about, stand by

entries.meaning: Deliberately look for someone or something until you get to them — the effort is the whole point.
examples: Reporters sought out the families before the names were released.
She seeks out the hardest route on every climb.
If you're new here, seek the old-timers out — they know where everything is.
He has always sought out work that scares him a little.
Good editors don't wait for talent; they seek it out.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — seek out new clients or seek new clients out; with a pronoun it must split: seek them out.
entries.register: formal — a written, deliberate word; in speech Americans usually say go find or track down
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the deliberate effort is the whole meaning, and it takes the progressive: she's seeking out the hardest route.
entries.passive: yes, and common in writing — the families were sought out before the names were released.
entries.see also: see about, shake down, stand out

entries.meaning: Get rid of property or stock by selling it, usually fast and often cheap.
examples: The chain is selling off its stores in the Midwest.
They sold the furniture off piece by piece to make rent.
After the merger the new owners sold off everything that wasn't profitable.
He kept the guitars and sold the rest off.
The fund had to sell them off at a loss.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — sell off the assets or sell the assets off; with a pronoun it must split: sell them off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a disposal carried out over a stretch of time: the chain is selling off its stores.
entries.passive: yes — everything that wasn't profitable was sold off after the merger.
entries.see also: sell out, sell up, sell out of

entries.meaning: Persuade someone to accept an idea, a plan, or a person.
examples: It took a month to sell the board on the new schedule.
You don't have to sell me on her — I've seen her work.
He sold us on the neighborhood by walking us through it at night.
I was never really sold on the idea.
Sell them on the price first; the features can wait.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress and on is reduced to /ən/ — SOLD me on it
entries.separable: the person you are persuading always sits between the verb and on, and what you are persuading them of follows it: sell the board on the plan, sell me on it. ✗ sell on me the plan.
entries.transitive: yes — two objects: sell someone on something
entries.register: everyday — American, and everywhere in business talk
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; persuasion is something you do to someone, and it takes the progressive: he's still selling us on the neighborhood.
entries.passive: yes, and the participle is the commonest shape of all — I was never really sold on the idea.
entries.see also: sell short, sell out, speak up for

entries.meaning: Have your whole stock bought up — or betray people, or your own principles, for money.
examples: The first two shows sold out in an hour.
Get there early; that place sells out by noon.
He sold out his own crew for a lighter sentence.
She'd sell her own brother out to close a deal.
They sold us out the minute the money showed up.
Fans said the band sold out when the song turned up in a car ad.
You can call it selling out; I call it paying the mortgage.

senses.head: Be bought up completely
body: Of tickets, stock, or a show; usually with no object, and very often in the passive-looking sold out. (быть распроданным)
examples: The first two shows sold out in an hour.
Get there early; that place sells out by noon.

senses.head: Betray someone for your own gain
body: Separable, and the pronoun splits it: sold us out. (предать, сдать)
examples: He sold out his own crew for a lighter sentence.
She'd sell her own brother out to close a deal.
They sold us out the minute the money showed up.

senses.head: Abandon your principles for money
body: Disapproving, no object, and used constantly about bands, artists, and startups. (продаться)
examples: Fans said the band sold out when the song turned up in a car ad.
You can call it selling out; I call it paying the mortgage.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes in the betrayal sense — sell out your friends or sell your friends out, and with a pronoun it must split: sell them out. In the 'nothing left' sense there is no object to place at all: the show sold out.
entries.transitive: either — no object when tickets or stock run out, an object when you betray someone
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses; in sense 1 the participle has drifted toward an adjective of state, the show is sold out describing the condition rather than the event.
entries.passive: restricted — sense 2 passivizes freely: we were sold out by our own crew. Senses 1 and 3 take no object and so have no passive; the show sold out is active despite the look of sold out.
entries.see also: sell out of, sell off, sell short

entries.meaning: Have none of something left because it has all been sold.
examples: The bakery sells out of croissants by nine every Saturday.
We sold out of the blue ones in the first hour.
They had two hundred shirts and sold out of them before noon.
Order now — the store sold out of the first printing in a day.
Gas stations along the coast sold out of bottled water before the storm hit.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: we sold out of tickets, we sold out of them. ✗ sold tickets out of.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of state reached through selling, usually reported as a completed fact: they sold out of the blue ones by ten.
entries.passive: no — the noun after of cannot be promoted: ✗ croissants are sold out of by nine. Say the croissants sold out instead.
entries.see also: sell out, sell off

entries.meaning: Treat someone or something as worth less than they are — or, in finance, bet that a price will fall.
examples: Don't sell yourself short — you were the best candidate in the room.
People sell that little town short until they visit.
I sold him short, and he proved me wrong inside a week.
Two funds sold the airline short a week before the news broke.
He made his name selling banks short in 2008.

senses.head: Undervalue someone or something
body: Almost always negative, in the shape don't sell X short. (недооценивать)
examples: Don't sell yourself short — you were the best candidate in the room.
People sell that little town short until they visit.
I sold him short, and he proved me wrong inside a week.

senses.head: Bet that a stock will fall
body: Finance: borrow the shares, sell them now, buy them back cheaper later. (играть на понижение, шортить)
examples: Two funds sold the airline short a week before the news broke.
He made his name selling banks short in 2008.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and in the everyday sense it must split — whoever is being undervalued sits in the middle: don't sell yourself short, don't sell it short. ✗ don't sell short yourself.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, though sense 1 usually reports a standing judgment: people sell that town short until they visit.
entries.passive: yes — she was sold short by everyone who interviewed her; in finance, the airline was sold short a week before the news broke.
entries.see also: sell out, sell on, stick up for

entries.meaning: Sell your home or your business, usually in order to leave or retire.
examples: They sold up and moved to Portugal.
After the second bad year he sold up.
Her parents sold up in Leeds and never looked back.
If the rent goes up again, we'll sell up.
Half the shops on the high street have sold up since the factory closed.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object: they sold up and left.
entries.register: British — an American in the same situation says sold the house or sold the business
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single decisive act, and intransitive: after the second bad year he sold up.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the business was sold up.
entries.see also: sell off, sell out

entries.meaning: Make someone leave, or dispatch them somewhere far off — school, camp, treatment.
examples: She sent the kids away so the adults could talk.
He knocked twice and they sent him away.
They sent away the reporters who had gathered at the gate.
Their parents sent them away to boarding school at eleven.
They sent her away to her aunt's for the summer.
The company sent him away for six weeks of training.

senses.head: Make someone leave
body: Often curt: the person wanted something and did not get it. (прогнать, отослать)
examples: She sent the kids away so the adults could talk.
He knocked twice and they sent him away.
They sent away the reporters who had gathered at the gate.

senses.head: Dispatch someone to a distant place
body: Of boarding school, basic training, a rehab program — the person is put somewhere else for a stretch of time. (отправить, отослать)
examples: Their parents sent them away to boarding school at eleven.
They sent her away to her aunt's for the summer.
The company sent him away for six weeks of training.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — send away the applicants or send the applicants away; with a pronoun it must split: send them away, never ✗ send away them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 is durative in effect (the person stays away for a stretch) but the verb itself names the act of dispatching.
entries.passive: yes — the reporters at the gate were sent away; he was sent away to boarding school at eleven.
entries.see also: send away for, send back, send off, send out

entries.meaning: Order something by mail and wait for it to come.
examples: I sent away for a catalog and forgot about it.
As a kid he sent away for every free sample he saw.
You had to send away for the decoder ring and wait six weeks.
She sent away for the transcripts in September.
We sent away for it in March and it turned up in June.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: send away for a catalog, send away for it. ✗ send a catalog away for.
entries.register: everyday — slightly dated now that everything is ordered online
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; ordering by mail and then waiting, so it sits happily in the past: I sent away for a catalog and forgot about it.
entries.passive: no — the three-part string blocks the prepositional passive: ✗ a catalog was sent away for, ✗ the transcripts were sent away for in September.
entries.see also: send out for, send away, send for

entries.meaning: Return something to where it came from, usually because it is wrong.
examples: The steak was raw, so he sent it back.
Send back the form with both signatures.
They sent the shipment back unopened.
If the size is wrong, send them back within thirty days.
She sent the ring back in a padded envelope.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — send back the soup or send the soup back; with a pronoun it must split: send it back.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of return, often instantaneous: the steak was raw, so he sent it back.
entries.passive: yes — the shipment was sent back unopened; the form must be sent back with both signatures.
entries.see also: send off, send in, send out

entries.meaning: Move a player down to a lower league — or, in British use, expel a student or jail a criminal.
examples: The Mets sent him down to Triple-A in June.
They sent two pitchers down after the road trip.
He was sent down from Oxford in his second year.
The judge sent him down for six years.
He got sent down for fraud.

senses.head: Demote a player to the minors
body: Standard American baseball vocabulary. (отправить в низшую лигу)
examples: The Mets sent him down to Triple-A in June.
They sent two pitchers down after the road trip.

senses.head: Expel from a university
body: British only, and mostly Oxford and Cambridge; an American says expelled. (отчислить)
examples: He was sent down from Oxford in his second year.

senses.head: Send to prison
body: British and informal; an American judge puts someone away or gives them ten years. (упрятать за решётку)
examples: The judge sent him down for six years.
He got sent down for fraud.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отправить в низшую лигу; отчислить из университета; упрятать за решётку
entries.separable: yes — send him down, send down two pitchers; with a pronoun it must split: sent him down.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object, and it is very often passive: he was sent down
entries.register: everyday in the baseball sense (American); British in the university and prison senses
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — a demotion, an expulsion, a sentence.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the usual shape — he was sent down to Triple-A in June, he was sent down from Oxford in his second year, he got sent down for fraud.
entries.see also: send up, send away, send off

entries.meaning: Order or ask someone to come, or ask for something to be brought to you.
examples: Somebody send for a doctor.
They sent for her in the middle of the night.
The principal sent for both of them.
He sent for his family as soon as he had an apartment.
When the fever spiked, we sent for help.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: send for a doctor, send for her. ✗ send a doctor for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; summoning someone, and urgent by nature: when the fever spiked, we sent for help.
entries.passive: yes — one of the few prepositional verbs whose passive is fully idiomatic: a doctor was sent for immediately, she was sent for in the middle of the night.
entries.see also: send out for, send away for, send in

entries.meaning: Submit something to an office — or order people to go into a place.
examples: Send in your application before the first.
I sent it in on Friday and never heard back.
Three hundred readers sent photos in.
The governor sent in the National Guard.
The manager sent a pinch hitter in.

senses.head: Submit a document
body: Mail it, upload it, hand it over: the paperwork travels away from you toward whoever decides. (подать, прислать)
examples: Send in your application before the first.
I sent it in on Friday and never heard back.
Three hundred readers sent photos in.

senses.head: Order a person or a force to go in
body: Of troops, police, a relief pitcher, a substitute. (ввести, выпустить)
examples: The governor sent in the National Guard.
The manager sent a pinch hitter in.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — send in your application or send your application in; with a pronoun it must split: send it in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: submitting paperwork, and ordering people into a place.
entries.passive: yes — your application must be sent in before the first; the National Guard was sent in that night.
entries.see also: send off, send out, send back

entries.meaning: Mail something, wave someone off on a journey, or — in British soccer — throw a player out of the game.
examples: I sent off the check this morning.
Did you send the forms off yet?
She wrote it, sealed it, and sent it off before she could change her mind.
The whole block sent them off with a party.
The referee sent him off in the seventieth minute.

senses.head: Mail something
body: The commonest sense, and it carries a feeling of finality: once it is sent off it is out of your hands. (отправить по почте)
examples: I sent off the check this morning.
Did you send the forms off yet?
She wrote it, sealed it, and sent it off before she could change her mind.

senses.head: See someone off on a journey
body: The noun send-off is more common than the verb here: they gave him a great send-off. (проводить)
examples: The whole block sent them off with a party.

senses.head: Eject a player from a game
body: British soccer, and normally passive: he was sent off. American sports say ejected. (удалить с поля)
examples: The referee sent him off in the seventieth minute.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отправить (по почте); проводить; удалить с поля
entries.separable: yes — send off the check or send the check off; with a pronoun it must split: send it off.
entries.register: everyday; the soccer sense is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 carries a note of finality once the thing leaves your hands.
entries.passive: yes — the check was sent off this morning; sense 3 lives almost entirely in the passive, he was sent off in the seventieth minute.
entries.see also: send away, send in, see off, send out

entries.meaning: Distribute something to a lot of people at once, or give off heat, light, or a signal.
examples: We sent out the invitations in March.
They sent the invoices out twice by mistake.
The school sent them out to every parent in the district.
The beacon sends out a pulse every four seconds.
That little stove sends out more heat than the furnace does.

senses.head: Distribute widely
body: One sender, many recipients: invitations, invoices, a newsletter. (разослать)
examples: We sent out the invitations in March.
They sent the invoices out twice by mistake.
The school sent them out to every parent in the district.

senses.head: Give off heat, light, or a signal
body: The source radiates something outward. (испускать, издавать)
examples: The beacon sends out a pulse every four seconds.
That little stove sends out more heat than the furnace does.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — send out the invitations or send the invitations out; with a pronoun it must split: send them out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 (radiate heat, light, a signal) describes an ongoing process and takes the progressive naturally: the beacon is sending out a pulse every four seconds.
entries.passive: yes — the invitations were sent out in March; a pulse is sent out every four seconds. Sense 2 with a plain source is stilted in the passive: ✗ more heat is sent out by that little stove.
entries.see also: send out for, send in, send off, send away

entries.meaning: Order food to be brought to where you are.
examples: Nobody wanted to cook, so we sent out for pizza.
They send out for Thai every Friday.
It's late — should we send out for something?
The crew sent out for coffee at two in the morning.
We sent out for it instead of driving anywhere.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: send out for pizza, send out for it. ✗ send pizza out for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; ordering food to be brought to you, and habitual in the present: they send out for Thai every Friday.
entries.passive: no — the three-part string admits no passive: ✗ pizza was sent out for, ✗ coffee was sent out for at two in the morning.
entries.see also: send away for, send for, send off

entries.meaning: Put someone in prison — or make fun of someone by imitating them.
examples: They sent him up for ten years.
The same detective sent his brother up in the nineties.
He got sent up on a tax charge.
The show sends up local news anchors every week.
She sent the whole industry up in one four-minute sketch.

senses.head: Send to prison
body: American, informal, and slightly old-movie: they sent him up the river. (упрятать за решётку)
examples: They sent him up for ten years.
The same detective sent his brother up in the nineties.
He got sent up on a tax charge.

senses.head: Parody, make fun of
body: By imitation, usually affectionate. The noun is send-up. (спародировать)
examples: The show sends up local news anchors every week.
She sent the whole industry up in one four-minute sketch.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — send up the whole industry or send the whole industry up; with a pronoun it must split: sent him up.
entries.register: informal in the prison sense (American); everyday in the parody sense, though commoner in Britain
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: imprisoning someone, and parodying them.
entries.passive: yes — he got sent up on a tax charge; local news anchors are sent up on the show every week.
entries.see also: send down, send off, shoot down

entries.meaning: Start on a task and get into it — the emphasis is on how you go at it.
examples: She set about cleaning the garage the day she moved in.
He set about the repairs with more confidence than skill.
They set about it methodically, one room at a time.
Nobody knew how to set about telling him.
Two of them set about him in the parking lot.

senses.head: Begin a task
body: Nearly always followed by an -ing form, and usually with some description of the manner: methodically, cheerfully, with a crowbar. (приняться за, взяться за)
examples: She set about cleaning the garage the day she moved in.
He set about the repairs with more confidence than skill.
They set about it methodically, one room at a time.
Nobody knew how to set about telling him.

senses.head: Attack someone
body: British, and violent: they set about him with sticks. An American says jumped him. (наброситься на)
examples: Two of them set about him in the parking lot.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object, usually an -ing form, follows the preposition: set about fixing it, set about it. ✗ set it about.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and inceptive — it names the beginning of a task, which is why it takes an -ing complement: she set about cleaning the garage.
entries.passive: no in American use — the -ing clause cannot be promoted: ✗ cleaning the garage was set about. Only the British 'attack' sense passivizes: he was set about in the parking lot.
entries.see also: set to, set out, see about

entries.meaning: Make someone or something noticeably different from all the rest — almost always better.
examples: What sets her apart is that she actually listens.
The sauce is what sets this place apart from every other diner in town.
Patience is what sets apart the best teachers from the rest.
One small detail sets the two paintings apart.
His patience set him apart from the other coaches.
It's a good design; the finish is what sets it apart.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — set apart the best students or set the best students apart; with a pronoun it must split: what sets it apart, never ✗ what sets apart it.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object, usually with from
entries.verb type: action in form but stative in meaning — it states a standing difference rather than an event, and resists the progressive: ✗ patience is setting the best teachers apart.
entries.passive: yes, though far less common than the active what sets her apart — she is set apart by her patience, the two paintings are set apart by one small detail.
entries.see also: stand out, set aside, show off

entries.meaning: Keep something back for later, put a question off for now, or — in court — cancel a decision.
examples: We set aside a little every month.
She set two hours aside for the call.
Set it aside for the kids' tuition.
Let's set aside the budget question until Monday.
An appeals court set the verdict aside in March.

senses.head: Save for later
body: Of money, time, or a portion of anything. (откладывать)
examples: We set aside a little every month.
She set two hours aside for the call.
Set it aside for the kids' tuition.

senses.head: Put a question out of the way for now
body: You are not answering it; you are agreeing not to argue about it yet. (оставить в стороне)
examples: Let's set aside the budget question until Monday.

senses.head: Annul a legal decision
body: Formal and legal: a higher court cancels what a lower one decided. (отменить решение суда)
examples: An appeals court set the verdict aside in March.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: откладывать (деньги, время); оставить в стороне; отменить (решение суда)
entries.separable: yes — set aside two hours or set two hours aside; with a pronoun it must split: set it aside.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: saving something, shelving a question, annulling a judgment.
entries.passive: yes — two hours were set aside for the call; the verdict was set aside by an appeals court in March.
entries.see also: set apart, set back, sit on

entries.meaning: Push progress backward — or, informally, cost someone a painful amount of money.
examples: The storm set the schedule back a month.
One bad quarter set back years of careful work.
Losing the permit set us back badly.
That watch must have set him back a thousand dollars.
The repairs set me back more than the car is worth.

senses.head: Delay progress
body: The subject is the setback: a storm, a strike, a bad quarter. The noun setback comes straight from it. (задержать, отбросить назад)
examples: The storm set the schedule back a month.
One bad quarter set back years of careful work.
Losing the permit set us back badly.

senses.head: Cost someone money
body: Informal, and always with a sum: set me back forty bucks. (обойтись в)
examples: That watch must have set him back a thousand dollars.
The repairs set me back more than the car is worth.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and with a person or a pronoun it must split: set us back, set the project back six months. With a long noun object either order works: set back the whole schedule.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1 (a delay is something that happens to progress); sense 2 (cost money) is stative, a cost-type verb, and rejects the progressive: ✗ that watch is setting him back a thousand dollars.
entries.passive: restricted — sense 1 passivizes: the schedule was set back a month by the storm. Sense 2 behaves like cost and refuses it: ✗ a thousand dollars was set him back, ✗ he was set back a thousand dollars by that watch.
entries.see also: set aside, set off, speed up

entries.meaning: Put something down onto a surface, write something down for the record, or land an aircraft.
examples: She set the tray down without a sound.
Set it down over there by the door.
The rules were set down in 1912 and never revised.
He set down everything he could remember that night.
The pilot set the helicopter down in a parking lot.

senses.head: Put down onto a surface
body: Gentler and more deliberate than put down. (поставить, опустить)
examples: She set the tray down without a sound.
Set it down over there by the door.

senses.head: Write down for the record
body: Formal: rules, terms, and testimony are set down, usually in the passive. (записать, изложить)
examples: The rules were set down in 1912 and never revised.
He set down everything he could remember that night.

senses.head: Land an aircraft
body: Aviation, transitive: the pilot is the subject. (посадить самолёт)
examples: The pilot set the helicopter down in a parking lot.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — set down the tray or set the tray down; with a pronoun it must split: set it down.
entries.register: everyday; the 'record in writing' sense is formal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: lowering something, recording it, landing an aircraft.
entries.passive: yes — the rules were set down in 1912 and never revised; the helicopter was set down in a parking lot.
entries.see also: set forth, set out, set up

entries.meaning: State something formally in writing — or, in older writing, start out on a journey.
examples: The conditions are set forth in section four.
The memo sets forth three options and recommends the second.
He set forth his reasons at considerable length.
The statute sets them forth in order of priority.
They set forth at first light with two mules.

senses.head: State formally in writing
body: The natural verb for contracts, statutes, and memos. (изложить)
examples: The conditions are set forth in section four.
The memo sets forth three options and recommends the second.
He set forth his reasons at considerable length.
The statute sets them forth in order of priority.

senses.head: Start a journey
body: Literary and a little grand; set out is the everyday word. (отправиться в путь)
examples: They set forth at first light with two mules.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, though in the written sense the object nearly always follows the particle: set forth the terms. A pronoun still splits it: set them forth in order. In the travel sense there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object in the 'state' sense, none in the 'depart' sense
entries.register: formal — legal and literary; in speech Americans say lay out or spell out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is a formal act of statement, sense 2 a departure.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1, and that is where the phrase usually lives — the conditions are set forth in section four. Sense 2 takes no object: ✗ first light was set forth at.
entries.see also: set out, set down, speak to

entries.meaning: Begin and then settle in for a while — said almost entirely of unwelcome things.
examples: The rain set in around noon and never let up.
Panic set in when the lights went out.
Rot had already set in behind the siding.
Winter sets in early that far north.
By the third hour, boredom had set in.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: наступить, установиться (о погоде, поре); начаться и затянуться
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it never takes an object: winter set in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: it names the onset of a condition that then persists. Intransitive, and the progressive is odd: ✗ the rain is setting in is possible but rare beside the rain set in.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ panic was set in, ✗ the rain was set in around noon.
entries.see also: set off, spring up, sink in

entries.meaning: Start out on a trip, make something go off, or make something look better by contrast.
examples: We set off at dawn.
They set off for the coast without a map.
Burnt toast set off the smoke alarm.
She set the alarm off climbing back in through the window.
One innocent question set him off for twenty minutes.
Somebody set it off in the middle of the night.
The dark frame really sets off the painting.

senses.head: Start a journey
body: No object; usually with for plus the destination. (отправиться в путь)
examples: We set off at dawn.
They set off for the coast without a map.

senses.head: Trigger or detonate
body: Alarms, fireworks, arguments, and people all get set off. (вызвать, привести в действие)
examples: Burnt toast set off the smoke alarm.
She set the alarm off climbing back in through the window.
One innocent question set him off for twenty minutes.
Somebody set it off in the middle of the night.

senses.head: Make something look better by contrast
body: Of a frame, a color, a setting. (оттенить, подчеркнуть)
examples: The dark frame really sets off the painting.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отправиться в путь; вызвать, привести в действие; оттенить, подчеркнуть
entries.separable: yes in the 'trigger' sense — set off the alarm or set the alarm off, and a pronoun must split: set it off. In the 'depart' sense there is no object.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you leave, an object when you trigger something
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: departing, triggering, and heightening by contrast (sense 3 reports a standing effect: the dark frame sets off the painting).
entries.passive: restricted — senses 2 and 3 passivize freely: the smoke alarm was set off by burnt toast, the painting is set off by the dark frame. Sense 1 has no object and no passive: ✗ the coast was set off for.
entries.see also: set out, set in, set up, shoot up

entries.meaning: Start a journey, start out intending something, or lay something out clearly.
examples: They set out before sunrise.
She set out from Boston with two hundred dollars and an address.
He never set out to be famous.
We set out to build something small.
The report sets out the risks in plain language.
Set the tools out where you can see them.
She set them out on the table in order of size.

senses.head: Start a journey
body: No object; the everyday partner of the literary set forth. (отправиться)
examples: They set out before sunrise.
She set out from Boston with two hundred dollars and an address.

senses.head: set out to do — intend from the start
body: Always with an infinitive, and often used to say that what happened was not the plan. (поставить себе целью)
examples: He never set out to be famous.
We set out to build something small.

senses.head: State or arrange clearly
body: Of an argument on paper or objects on a table. (изложить; разложить)
examples: The report sets out the risks in plain language.
Set the tools out where you can see them.
She set them out on the table in order of size.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отправиться; поставить себе целью; изложить; разложить, расставить
entries.separable: yes when it means state or arrange — set out the terms or set the terms out, and a pronoun splits it: set them out. In the 'depart' and set out to do senses there is no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout; sense 2 (set out to do) states an intention held from the start and appears mostly in the past: he never set out to be famous.
entries.passive: restricted — sense 3 passivizes and often prefers it: the risks are set out in plain language, the tools were set out in order of size. Senses 1 and 2 take no object: ✗ sunrise was set out before.
entries.see also: set off, set forth, set about, set up

entries.meaning: Start working, or eating, with real energy.
examples: They set to and had the fence up by noon.
He rolled up his sleeves and set to.
The crew set to with shovels and a wheelbarrow.
Set to, everyone — dinner's getting cold.
She set to on the dishes without being asked.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.register: rare — old-fashioned; common in older writing, but today an American says got to work or dug in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: starting in on work or food with energy, and often an imperative: set to, everyone.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ the dishes were set to.
entries.see also: set about, set out, stick with

entries.meaning: Put something in place and get it working — a business, a tent, a meeting — or frame someone for a crime.
examples: They set up the company in a garage.
She set up a scholarship in her mother's name.
It takes an hour to set the tent up.
Can you set it up before the guests arrive?
I'll set up a call for Thursday morning.
His sister set him up with her roommate.
He swears the whole thing was a set-up and that somebody set him up.

senses.head: Establish, found
body: Of a company, a fund, a committee. (основать, учредить)
examples: They set up the company in a garage.
She set up a scholarship in her mother's name.

senses.head: Assemble, get ready
body: Physical: the parts exist and you put them together. (собрать, наладить)
examples: It takes an hour to set the tent up.
Can you set it up before the guests arrive?

senses.head: Arrange a meeting or an introduction
body: Set someone up with is the standard way to describe a blind date. (устроить, организовать)
examples: I'll set up a call for Thursday morning.
His sister set him up with her roommate.

senses.head: Frame someone
body: Informal, and usually passive: I was set up. (подставить)
examples: He swears the whole thing was a set-up and that somebody set him up.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: основать, учредить; собрать, наладить; устроить (встречу); подставить
entries.separable: yes — set up the tent or set the tent up; with a pronoun it must split: set it up, never ✗ set up it.
entries.transitive: either — usually transitive; set up on your own takes no object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: founding, assembling, arranging, framing.
entries.passive: yes, and heavily used — the company was set up in a garage; a call has been set up for Thursday; sense 4 is passive by default, I was set up.
entries.see also: set out, set about, stand up, shut down

entries.meaning: Attack someone suddenly, usually several against one.
examples: He was set upon by three men outside the station.
The hikers were set upon by a pack of dogs.
They set upon the caravan at dusk.
She was set upon before she could reach the gate.
The gulls set upon the fries the second he looked away.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition, and the phrase is usually passive: he was set upon by three men. ✗ set him upon.
entries.register: formal — rare and literary; the everyday American words are jumped and attacked
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a sudden attack, and punctual rather than durative.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is where the phrase actually lives — he was set upon by three men outside the station, the hikers were set upon by a pack of dogs.
entries.see also: set about, swing at, strike back

entries.meaning: Squeeze money out of someone, search a place roughly, or give something new a trial run.
examples: They shook down every shop on the block for protection money.
He shook the kid down for his lunch money.
The inspector shook them down twice a year.
Guards shook down the cells after the fight.
We shook the new boat down on a short run out to the island.

senses.head: Extort money
body: The commonest sense, and the source of the noun shakedown. (вытрясти деньги, обобрать)
examples: They shook down every shop on the block for protection money.
He shook the kid down for his lunch money.
The inspector shook them down twice a year.

senses.head: Search thoroughly and roughly
body: Of cells, cars, and apartments — police and prison vocabulary. (обыскать, перетрясти)
examples: Guards shook down the cells after the fight.

senses.head: Give something a trial run
body: From the shakedown cruise of a new ship: run it hard and see what falls off. (обкатать)
examples: We shook the new boat down on a short run out to the island.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: вытрясти деньги, обобрать; обыскать, перетрясти; обкатать
entries.separable: yes — shake down the shopkeepers or shake the shopkeepers down; with a pronoun it must split: shook him down.
entries.register: informal — American, and slightly criminal in flavor
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: extorting, searching, and giving something a trial run.
entries.passive: yes — every shop on the block was shaken down for protection money; the cells were shaken down after the fight.
entries.see also: shake up, shake out, stick up

entries.meaning: Get rid of something that is clinging to you — an illness, a mood, a slump, or a pursuer.
examples: I can't seem to shake off this cough.
She shook the nerves off as soon as the music started.
It took him a week to shake it off.
He shook off the defender at the top of the key.
They shook the tail off somewhere near the bridge.

senses.head: Get rid of an illness or a feeling
body: The thing is stuck to you and you are trying to make it let go. Shake it off on its own means 'never mind that'. (избавиться от, стряхнуть)
examples: I can't seem to shake off this cough.
She shook the nerves off as soon as the music started.
It took him a week to shake it off.

senses.head: Escape someone following you
body: Of a defender, a tail, a reputation. (оторваться от, отделаться от)
examples: He shook off the defender at the top of the key.
They shook the tail off somewhere near the bridge.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: избавиться от (простуды, настроения); оторваться от преследования
entries.separable: yes — shake off a cold or shake a cold off; with a pronoun it must split: shake it off, never ✗ shake off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; getting something to let go of you, and it takes the progressive: he's still shaking off the flu.
entries.passive: restricted — the active is strongly preferred; the passive is possible with a pursuer, the defender was shaken off at the top of the key, but stilted with an illness: ✗ this cough can't be shaken off.
entries.see also: shake up, sleep off, stick with

entries.meaning: Seal an agreement by shaking hands on it.
examples: We agreed on a price and shook on it.
Let's shake on it and go get lunch.
They shook on the deal before the lawyers ever saw it.
He wouldn't shake on it, which told me plenty.
Nothing was ever signed; we just shook on it.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition, and in practice it is always it: shake on it. ✗ shake it on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single ceremonial act, and the object is always it: we agreed on a price and shook on it.
entries.passive: no — the fixed it leaves nothing to promote and the prepositional passive fails: ✗ it was shaken on, ✗ the deal was shaken on.
entries.see also: stand by, stick to, swear to

entries.meaning: Shake something to clear it or open it out — or, of a situation, settle into its final shape.
examples: Shake out the rug before you roll it up.
He shook the towel out and hung it on the line.
Take the tent down and shake it out.
Let's see how the schedule shakes out.
However it shakes out, we'll be fine.

senses.head: Shake something clean or open
body: Rugs, towels, tents, sleeping bags. (вытряхнуть, встряхнуть)
examples: Shake out the rug before you roll it up.
He shook the towel out and hung it on the line.
Take the tent down and shake it out.

senses.head: how things shake out — how they end up
body: American and informal, with no object; used when the outcome is still moving. (как всё сложится, утрясётся)
examples: Let's see how the schedule shakes out.
However it shakes out, we'll be fine.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: вытряхнуть, встряхнуть; сложиться, утрястись (о развитии событий)
entries.separable: yes in the literal sense — shake out the rug or shake the rug out, and a pronoun must split: shake it out. The 'how things turn out' sense takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 (how things shake out) describes an outcome settling into place and is usually future-looking: let's see how the schedule shakes out.
entries.passive: restricted — the literal sense passivizes: the rug was shaken out on the porch. Sense 2 takes no object and has no passive: ✗ the schedule was shaken out.
entries.see also: shake down, shake up, spread out

entries.meaning: Badly upset someone, or reorganize an institution from top to bottom.
examples: The crash shook her up more than she admitted.
He was pretty shaken up afterward.
It shook us up for a few days.
The new owner shook up the whole front office.
They shook the department up and half the staff quit.

senses.head: Upset or shock someone
body: Very often passive — shaken up is the standard way to describe someone after a crash. (потрясти, выбить из колеи)
examples: The crash shook her up more than she admitted.
He was pretty shaken up afterward.
It shook us up for a few days.

senses.head: Reorganize drastically
body: Of a company, a roster, a department; the noun is shake-up. (встряхнуть, реорганизовать)
examples: The new owner shook up the whole front office.
They shook the department up and half the staff quit.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: потрясти, выбить из колеи; встряхнуть, реорганизовать
entries.separable: yes — shake up the front office or shake the front office up; with a pronoun it must split: it shook us up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; in sense 1 the participle has hardened into an adjective of state — he was pretty shaken up describes how he was, not what was done to him.
entries.passive: yes, and sense 1 is normally passive — she was shaken up by the crash; the whole front office was shaken up by the new owner.
entries.see also: shake down, shake off, set up

entries.meaning: Be plainly visible in spite of everything on top of it — said of a quality, not a light.
examples: Her enthusiasm shines through in every lesson.
The book is uneven, but the affection for the place shines through.
He was exhausted, and it shone through anyway.
Whatever the arrangement, her voice shines through the mix.
Good training shines through under pressure.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate in the ordinary use — it takes no object: her talent shines through. When an object does follow, through is a preposition and never splits: shines through the writing.
entries.verb type: action in form, but it reports a persisting quality rather than an event — closest to stative in feel, though the progressive is fine: her enthusiasm is shining through.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in its ordinary use, and where a noun follows, through is a preposition that will not passivize: ✗ the mix was shone through by her voice.
entries.see also: stand out, stick out, show up

entries.meaning: Bring an aircraft down with gunfire — or reject an idea flatly and publicly.
examples: Two helicopters were shot down that night.
They shot the drone down over the harbor.
The committee shot down every proposal I made.
He shot it down before I finished the sentence.
Don't shoot the idea down just because it's cheap.

senses.head: Destroy an aircraft in flight
body: The literal military sense, usually passive. (сбить)
examples: Two helicopters were shot down that night.
They shot the drone down over the harbor.

senses.head: Reject an idea flatly
body: The figurative sense is far commoner in daily life, and it always implies bluntness. (зарубить, разнести в пух и прах)
examples: The committee shot down every proposal I made.
He shot it down before I finished the sentence.
Don't shoot the idea down just because it's cheap.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — shoot down the proposal or shoot the proposal down; with a pronoun it must split: he shot it down.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: destroying an aircraft, and rejecting an idea flatly.
entries.passive: yes — two helicopters were shot down that night; every proposal I made was shot down by the committee.
entries.see also: shoot up, send up, strike down

entries.meaning: Aim at a target — a date, a number, a level of ambition.
examples: We're shooting for a June launch.
Shoot for twenty pages a week and don't count the bad ones.
They're shooting for a hundred thousand by Friday.
I'd shoot for the earlier flight if I were you.
Shoot for the moon, as my grandmother used to say.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: стремиться к, метить в, ориентироваться на
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: shoot for a June launch, shoot for it. ✗ shoot a June launch for.
entries.register: informal — American; the neutral equivalent is aim for
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; aiming at a target, and comfortable in the progressive: we're shooting for a June launch.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not available: ✗ a June launch is being shot for, ✗ twenty pages a week were shot for.
entries.see also: set out, stick with, stand for

entries.meaning: Rise or grow very fast — or spray a place with bullets, or inject a drug.
examples: Prices shot up after the storm.
Her fever shot up overnight.
He shot up four inches over the summer.
They shot up the whole storefront and drove off.
Somebody shot the sign up years ago and nobody ever replaced it.
The place had been empty for years by the time somebody shot it up.
He'd been shooting up in the bathroom.

senses.head: Rise sharply
body: Of prices, temperatures, numbers. No object. (резко взлететь, подскочить)
examples: Prices shot up after the storm.
Her fever shot up overnight.

senses.head: Grow fast
body: Of children and plants. (вымахать, быстро вырасти)
examples: He shot up four inches over the summer.

senses.head: Riddle a place with bullets
body: Transitive and separable. (изрешетить, расстрелять)
examples: They shot up the whole storefront and drove off.
Somebody shot the sign up years ago and nobody ever replaced it.
The place had been empty for years by the time somebody shot it up.

senses.head: Inject a drug
body: Slang, and unambiguous in context. (ширяться, колоться)
examples: He'd been shooting up in the bathroom.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: резко взлететь (о ценах); быстро вырасти; изрешетить; колоться (сленг)
entries.separable: yes in the 'riddle with bullets' sense — shoot up the storefront or shoot the storefront up, and a pronoun splits it: shot it up. The 'rise sharply' and 'grow fast' senses take no object.
entries.register: everyday in the 'rise' and 'grow' senses; informal and drug slang in the last one
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: rising sharply, growing fast, riddling a place with bullets, injecting a drug.
entries.passive: restricted — only sense 3 has one, and it is common: the storefront was shot up and never repaired. Senses 1, 2, and 4 take no object: ✗ prices were shot up after the storm.
entries.see also: shoot down, spring up, spread out

entries.meaning: Take someone through a place and point things out as you go.
examples: I'll show you around before the meeting starts.
Sam showed the new hires around on Monday.
Would you show them around the plant?
Nobody showed her around, so she found the break room by smell.
He showed us around his workshop for the better part of an hour.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and the person nearly always sits in the middle: show the new hires around, show them around. ✗ show around them.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — the person, not the place
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: walking someone through a place and pointing things out. Progressive is normal — he's showing the new hires around.
entries.passive: yes — the new hires were shown around on Monday; she was never shown around, so she found the break room by smell.
entries.see also: show in, show out, show off

entries.meaning: Bring a visitor into the room where they are expected.
examples: Show him in.
The secretary showed us in and closed the door behind her.
Please show the next patient in.
They showed her in through the side entrance.
Don't leave him standing out there — show him in.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and with a person the object almost always sits inside: show him in, show the next patient in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of bringing a visitor into the room. Progressive is fine — the nurse is showing the next patient in.
entries.passive: yes — we were shown in and the door closed behind us; she was shown in through the side entrance.
entries.see also: show out, show around, see out

entries.meaning: Behave loudly to be admired, or display something you are proud of.
examples: He's only showing off because you're watching.
Quit showing off and eat your dinner.
She showed off her ring at every table.
He showed his new bike off to everyone on the block.
He brought the car by just to show it off.
The remodel finally gave them something to show off.

senses.head: Behave to attract attention
body: No object, and always disapproving; the noun show-off is the person who does it. (красоваться, выпендриваться)
examples: He's only showing off because you're watching.
Quit showing off and eat your dinner.

senses.head: Display something proudly
body: Transitive and separable; the thing displayed is genuinely worth looking at. (демонстрировать, похвастаться)
examples: She showed off her ring at every table.
He showed his new bike off to everyone on the block.
He brought the car by just to show it off.
The remodel finally gave them something to show off.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — show off the ring or show the ring off, and a pronoun must split: show it off. Behaving like a show-off takes no object at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: behaving loudly for attention (he's only showing off) and displaying something proudly (she showed off her ring). No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — the display sense passivizes: the ring was shown off at every table. The attention-seeking sense has no object at all: ✗ was shown off by him.
entries.see also: show up, stand out, set apart

entries.meaning: Walk a visitor to the door on their way out.
examples: Marcus, would you show Ms. Reyes out?
She showed him out without another word.
I know the way — I'll show myself out.
They showed the reporters out through the lobby.
He was shown out before he could finish the sentence.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and the person usually sits inside: show her out, I'll show myself out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: walking a visitor to the door. Progressive is normal — she's showing them out now.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry uses it — he was shown out before he could finish the sentence; the reporters were shown out through the lobby.
entries.see also: show in, see out, see off

entries.meaning: Arrive — especially when arriving was in doubt — or become visible, or make someone else look bad.
examples: He showed up two hours late with no explanation.
Half the class didn't show up.
Show up early if you want a seat.
The crack showed up on the scan.
Coffee stains show up on white.
The intern showed us up on her second day.
One honest answer showed the whole panel up.

senses.head: Arrive, turn up
body: The everyday American word for arriving; it carries a hint that showing up was not guaranteed. (появиться, прийти)
examples: He showed up two hours late with no explanation.
Half the class didn't show up.
Show up early if you want a seat.

senses.head: Become visible
body: Of marks, cracks, and results on a test or a scan. (проявиться, быть заметным)
examples: The crack showed up on the scan.
Coffee stains show up on white.

senses.head: Make someone look bad by comparison
body: Transitive, and the person always sits in the middle. (затмить, выставить в невыгодном свете)
examples: The intern showed us up on her second day.
One honest answer showed the whole panel up.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: появиться, прийти; проявиться, стать заметным; затмить, выставить в невыгодном свете
entries.separable: yes in the 'outshine' sense, where the person must sit inside: she showed him up. In the 'arrive' and 'become visible' senses there is no object to place.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: arriving (he showed up two hours late), becoming visible (the crack showed up on the scan), and outshining someone (the intern showed us up). Progressive is fine — nobody's showing up on time.
entries.passive: restricted — only the outshine sense has an object: the whole panel was shown up by one honest answer. The arrive and become-visible senses are objectless: ✗ the meeting was shown up to.
entries.see also: show off, shine through, stand out

entries.meaning: Put someone or something somewhere closed off from the rest of the world.
examples: He shuts himself away for a week before every deadline.
They shut the documents away in a safe.
She was shut away in a hospital for months.
Don't shut it away in a drawer where nobody will ever see it.
The dog gets shut away when guests come.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — shut away the documents or shut the documents away; with a pronoun or a reflexive it must split: shut it away, shuts himself away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: putting a person or a thing somewhere closed off. Progressive is normal — he's been shutting himself away for a week.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common — she was shut away in a hospital for months; the dog gets shut away when guests come.
entries.see also: shut off, shut out, shut down

entries.meaning: Close something for good, power a system off, or stop someone cold.
examples: They shut the mill down in 1994.
The city shut down two more clinics this spring.
Shut it down before you unplug anything.
The reactor shut down automatically.
She shut him down with one question.

senses.head: Close a business or plant permanently
body: The noun shutdown covers both the factory and the government kind. (закрыть, остановить)
examples: They shut the mill down in 1994.
The city shut down two more clinics this spring.

senses.head: Power a machine or system off
body: Also intransitive: the system shuts down at midnight. (выключить, отключить)
examples: Shut it down before you unplug anything.
The reactor shut down automatically.

senses.head: Stop someone cold
body: Informal: you end their argument, their advance, or their scoring. (осадить, заткнуть)
examples: She shut him down with one question.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — shut down the plant or shut the plant down; with a pronoun it must split: shut it down. Machines also shut down on their own, with no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: closing a plant, powering a system off, and stopping someone cold. The machine sense is also ergative — the system can shut down on its own with no agent named.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the mill was shut down in 1994; he was shut down with one question. No passive of the intransitive the reactor shut down automatically.
entries.see also: shut off, shut out, set up

entries.meaning: Stop a flow or a machine — or cut something off from contact with everything else.
examples: Shut off the water before you touch that pipe.
Somebody shut the gas off at the street.
Shut it off — the noise is making me crazy.
He shut himself off from everyone for a year.
The valley is shut off by snow for months at a time.

senses.head: Stop a flow or a machine
body: Water, gas, power, an engine, an alarm. (перекрыть, отключить)
examples: Shut off the water before you touch that pipe.
Somebody shut the gas off at the street.
Shut it off — the noise is making me crazy.

senses.head: Cut off from contact
body: Usually reflexive or passive: shut himself off, shut off by snow. (отгородиться, быть отрезанным)
examples: He shut himself off from everyone for a year.
The valley is shut off by snow for months at a time.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — shut off the water or shut the water off; with a pronoun it must split: shut it off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: stopping a flow or a machine, or cutting someone off from contact. Progressive is normal — they're shutting the water off at noon.
entries.passive: yes, and the second sense lives in it — the gas was shut off at the street; the valley is shut off by snow for months at a time.
entries.see also: shut down, shut out, shut away

entries.meaning: Keep something or someone outside — noise, light, a competitor — or hold an opponent to zero.
examples: Heavy curtains shut out most of the light.
She shut the noise out with a pair of earplugs.
They shut him out of the decision entirely.
The Yankees shut them out in both games.
He shut out the Sox for eight innings.

senses.head: Keep out, exclude
body: Physical (light, noise, cold) or social (a person left out of a decision). (не впускать, заглушать; исключить)
examples: Heavy curtains shut out most of the light.
She shut the noise out with a pair of earplugs.
They shut him out of the decision entirely.

senses.head: Hold an opponent scoreless
body: American sports; the noun shutout is a game in which one side scores nothing. (не дать забить, сыграть на ноль)
examples: The Yankees shut them out in both games.
He shut out the Sox for eight innings.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: не впускать, заглушать; исключить; не дать забить (спорт.)
entries.separable: yes — shut out the light or shut the light out; with a pronoun it must split: shut them out.
entries.register: everyday; the scoreless sense is American sports vocabulary
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: keeping something or someone out (heavy curtains shut out the light) and holding an opponent scoreless (he shut out the Sox).
entries.passive: yes — he was shut out of the decision entirely; the Sox were shut out for eight innings.
entries.see also: shut off, shut away, shut down

entries.meaning: Stop talking, make someone else stop talking, or close a building for the season.
examples: Shut up and listen for one minute.
I wish he'd shut up about the boat.
That answer shut him up for the rest of the meeting.
One question from the back shut the whole room up.
Nothing shuts them up faster than the truth.
They shut up the cabin every October.

senses.head: Stop talking
body: No object. As a command it is genuinely rude — be quiet is what you say to a stranger. (замолчать, заткнуться)
examples: Shut up and listen for one minute.
I wish he'd shut up about the boat.

senses.head: Make someone stop talking
body: Transitive and separable; the subject is usually a fact, an argument, or a look. (заставить замолчать)
examples: That answer shut him up for the rest of the meeting.
One question from the back shut the whole room up.
Nothing shuts them up faster than the truth.

senses.head: Close a building
body: Of a shop at night or a cabin for the winter. (запереть, закрыть)
examples: They shut up the cabin every October.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes when it has an object — that shut him up, shut up the cabin or shut the cabin up. Told to a person as a command it takes no object at all.
entries.register: informal — rude and aggressive when aimed at a person; the 'close a building' sense is everyday
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: stopping talking, making someone stop, and closing a building for the season. No stative use.
entries.passive: restricted — the two transitive senses passivize, the building one comfortably: the cabin gets shut up every October; he was shut up for the rest of the meeting is possible but stiff. The command shut up and listen has no object and no passive.
entries.see also: shut down, shut away, speak up

entries.meaning: Join in with music that is already playing.
examples: Everybody sang along with the chorus.
She sings along to the radio the whole way to work.
Don't be shy — sing along.
Half the theater was singing along by the second verse.
He knows every word and sings along anyway, badly.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object; what you sing along to comes after with or to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: joining in with music already playing. Progressive is normal — half the theater was singing along.
entries.passive: no — it takes no object; what you sing along to sits behind with or to, and that will not promote: ✗ the chorus was sung along with.
entries.see also: sing out, speak up

entries.meaning: Call out loudly enough for someone to hear you.
examples: Just sing out if you need anything.
Somebody sang out from the back of the room.
Sing out when you're ready and I'll start the clock.
He sang out a warning about a second too late.
Don't wander off — sing out every few minutes so I know where you are.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: it hardly ever takes an object; when it does, the object follows the particle: sang out a warning.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: calling out loudly. Almost always objectless, and the rare object (sang out a warning) is still a plain act.
entries.passive: no in ordinary use — the objectless use has nothing to promote, and the rare object resists: ✗ a warning was sung out by him. Keep it active.
entries.see also: sing along, speak up, stick around

entries.meaning: Be absorbed — by the ground, or by a person's understanding.
examples: It took a week for the news to sink in.
He nodded, but you could tell it hadn't sunk in.
Give it a minute to sink in.
Water the beds slowly and let it sink in.
The stain had sunk in before anyone noticed it.

senses.head: Be understood at last
body: The news arrives first and the meaning arrives later; that gap is what sink in names. (дойти до сознания, уложиться в голове)
examples: It took a week for the news to sink in.
He nodded, but you could tell it hadn't sunk in.
Give it a minute to sink in.

senses.head: Soak into a surface
body: The literal sense, of water, oil, or a stain. (впитаться)
examples: Water the beds slowly and let it sink in.
The stain had sunk in before anyone noticed it.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: дойти (до сознания), уложиться в голове; впитаться
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object: it hasn't sunk in yet.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but a process rather than a deed: meaning arriving late (it took a week to sink in) or liquid soaking into a surface. Progressive is normal — it's starting to sink in.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the news was sunk in.
entries.see also: sink into, set in, shine through

entries.meaning: Settle down into something soft, drift into a bad state, or pour money into something.
examples: She sank into the armchair and closed her eyes.
His boots sank into the mud with every step.
The town sank into a long decline after the plant closed.
He sank into a depression that winter.
They sank a fortune into that restaurant.

senses.head: Settle down into something soft
body: The literal sense, of chairs, mud, snow. (погрузиться в, опуститься в)
examples: She sank into the armchair and closed her eyes.
His boots sank into the mud with every step.

senses.head: Drift into a bad state
body: Of depression, decline, silence, debt — always downward. (впасть в, погрузиться в)
examples: The town sank into a long decline after the plant closed.
He sank into a depression that winter.

senses.head: Pour money or effort into something
body: Transitive, with the money named first, and usually with a note of waste. (вложить, ухнуть)
examples: They sank a fortune into that restaurant.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: погрузиться в, опуститься в; впасть в; вложить (деньги) в
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: sink into a chair, sink into it. In the money sense a second object comes first (sink a fortune into the place), but nothing ever goes between sink and into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: settling into something soft, drifting into a bad state, or pouring money in. The middle sense is a gradual change of state, not a state: the town was sinking into a long decline.
entries.passive: restricted — only the money sense has a promotable object: a fortune was sunk into that restaurant. The settle and drift senses give nothing: ✗ the armchair was sunk into, ✗ a depression was sunk into.
entries.see also: sink in, set in

entries.meaning: Spend time doing nothing, usually longer than you should.
