examples: We sat around all afternoon waiting for a callback.
Don't just sit around — call somebody.
He sits around the shop reading the paper.
They sat around complaining about the weather.
I'm not going to sit around while she does all the work.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, even though the activity is doing nothing; the progressive is where it lives: we were sitting around all afternoon.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, with no object anywhere: ✗ the shop is sat around by him.
entries.see also: sit back, stick around, stand around

entries.meaning: Settle back and relax — or, in the sharper sense, do nothing while something happens.
examples: Sit back and let somebody else drive for once.
He sat back with his hands behind his head.
We can't just sit back and watch it happen.
She sat back and let them argue it out.
Nobody is going to sit back through another year of this.

senses.head: Relax and stop working
body: Literally leaning back, and figuratively letting other people carry it. (откинуться, расслабиться)
examples: Sit back and let somebody else drive for once.
He sat back with his hands behind his head.

senses.head: Do nothing while something happens
body: Always a criticism, and usually paired with and watch. (сидеть сложа руки)
examples: We can't just sit back and watch it happen.
She sat back and let them argue it out.
Nobody is going to sit back through another year of this.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: leaning back to relax, and standing by while something happens. Progressive is normal — you're just sitting back and letting it happen.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; there is nothing to promote: ✗ it was sat back and watched.
entries.see also: sit around, stand back, stand by

entries.meaning: Be present without being a participant — at a meeting, at a protest, or on a bandstand.
examples: Do you mind if I sit in?
A lawyer sat in while they took the statement.
She asked to sit in and ended up running the meeting.
Students sat in for three days outside the president's office.
The trumpet player sat in for a couple of numbers.

senses.head: Attend without taking part
body: You are in the room but not in the discussion; the fuller form is sit in on. (поприсутствовать)
examples: Do you mind if I sit in?
A lawyer sat in while they took the statement.
She asked to sit in and ended up running the meeting.

senses.head: Occupy a place in protest
body: The source of the noun sit-in. (устроить сидячую забастовку)
examples: Students sat in for three days outside the president's office.

senses.head: Play with a band as a guest
body: Music, and always a compliment. (подыграть, поиграть с группой)
examples: The trumpet player sat in for a couple of numbers.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: поприсутствовать (без участия); устроить сидячую забастовку; подыграть (с группой)
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object; what you sit in on follows on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: attending as an observer, occupying a place in protest, and guesting with a band. Progressive is normal — a lawyer was sitting in while they took the statement.
entries.passive: no — objectless; what you attend follows on, which is the separate [sit in on]: ✗ the meeting was sat in.
entries.see also: sit in on, sit in for, sit through

entries.meaning: Take someone's place for a short time.
examples: She's sitting in for the regular host this week.
Can you sit in for me on Thursday?
A deputy sat in for the mayor at the ceremony.
I sat in for him twice and never got so much as a thank-you.
Somebody has to sit in for her while she's out.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: sit in for the host, sit in for her. ✗ sit the host in for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: temporarily taking someone's place. Progressive is the usual tense — she's sitting in for the regular host this week.
entries.passive: no in practice — the three-part passive is not idiomatic here: ✗ the mayor was sat in for by a deputy. American usage keeps it active, or switches to stand in for.
entries.see also: stand in for, sit in, stand in

entries.meaning: Attend a class or a meeting as an observer rather than a participant.
examples: I sat in on two of her lectures.
Would you mind if I sit in on the interview?
He sat in on it just to hear what they'd say.
Parents can sit in on any class they like.
A translator sat in on every session.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: sit in on the meeting, sit in on it. ✗ sit the meeting in on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: attending a class or a meeting as an observer. Progressive is fine — a translator is sitting in on every session.
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part passive is marginal at best: ?every session was sat in on by a translator. All five entry examples are active, and that is the safe form.
entries.see also: sit in, sit in for, sit through

entries.meaning: Keep something and do nothing with it, serve on a committee, or quietly kill a story.
examples: They've been sitting on my application for a month.
Don't sit on it — send it out today.
The studio sat on the film for two years.
She sits on the zoning board.
The story got sat on before it ever ran.

senses.head: Delay dealing with something
body: The paperwork is on someone's desk and nothing is happening to it. (тянуть с решением, класть под сукно)
examples: They've been sitting on my application for a month.
Don't sit on it — send it out today.
The studio sat on the film for two years.

senses.head: Serve as a member of a body
body: Of boards, juries, and committees. (входить в состав, заседать в)
examples: She sits on the zoning board.

senses.head: Suppress something
body: Informal: a story, a complaint, or a person gets sat on. (замять, придавить)
examples: The story got sat on before it ever ran.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: тянуть с решением, класть под сукно; входить в состав (комиссии); придавить, замять
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: sit on the application, sit on it. ✗ sit the application on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the delay and suppress senses (they've been sitting on my application for a month). The committee sense is close to stative — a standing position rather than an act: she sits on the zoning board.
entries.passive: yes in the delay and suppress senses, and the entry uses it — the story got sat on before it ever ran; my application has been sat on for a month. Not in the membership sense: ✗ the zoning board is sat on by her.
entries.see also: set aside, shut down

entries.meaning: Stay out of something for once — or wait somewhere safe until it is over.
examples: He sat out the second half with a sprained ankle.
I think I'm going to sit this one out.
She sat the whole election out.
We sat out the storm in the basement.
They sat it out for three hours in the terminal.

senses.head: Not take part
body: Of a game, a dance, an election, a round of drinks. (пропустить, не участвовать)
examples: He sat out the second half with a sprained ankle.
I think I'm going to sit this one out.
She sat the whole election out.

senses.head: Wait until something is over
body: Of a storm, a delay, a bad stretch — you endure it in place. (пересидеть, переждать)
examples: We sat out the storm in the basement.
They sat it out for three hours in the terminal.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — sit out the next round or sit the next round out; with a pronoun it must split: sit this one out, sit it out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: skipping a round or a game, and waiting somewhere until something passes. Progressive is normal — he's sitting out the second half.
entries.passive: restricted — possible but stilted, and rare in speech: ?the whole election was sat out, ?the storm was sat out in the basement. American usage keeps this one active.
entries.see also: sit through, stick out, stand by

entries.meaning: Stay to the end of something long and dull.
examples: We sat through four hours of speeches.
Nobody should have to sit through that twice.
She sat through the whole rehearsal without complaining once.
I sat through it out of politeness.
He sat through the entire meeting and said exactly one word.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no, and this is the classic contrast with sit out. Sit through the whole lecture can never become ✗ sit the whole lecture through, and a pronoun stays put as well: sit through it, ✗ sit it through.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: enduring something long to the end. Progressive works — we were sitting through the fourth hour of speeches.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but stiff: ?four hours of speeches were sat through. It is commonest with a modal — that video has to be sat through twice.
entries.see also: sit out, stick out, sit in on

entries.meaning: Raise yourself into a sitting position, stay up late, or suddenly pay attention.
examples: He sat up in bed and turned on the lamp.
Sit up straight — you'll wreck your back.
She sat up half the night grading papers.
They sat up with him until the fever broke.
Those numbers made the board sit up and take notice.

senses.head: Raise yourself to sitting
body: From lying down, or from a slouch: sit up straight. (сесть, приподняться)
examples: He sat up in bed and turned on the lamp.
Sit up straight — you'll wreck your back.

senses.head: Stay up late
body: Usually because you are working or waiting for someone. (не ложиться, засидеться)
examples: She sat up half the night grading papers.
They sat up with him until the fever broke.

senses.head: sit up and take notice — suddenly pay attention
body: A fixed phrase; the subject is jolted out of indifference. (насторожиться, встрепенуться)
examples: Those numbers made the board sit up and take notice.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: сесть, приподняться; не ложиться спать; насторожиться
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: raising yourself to sitting, staying up late, and the fixed sit up and take notice. Progressive is fine for the second — she was sitting up half the night grading papers.
entries.passive: no — every sense is objectless, and the idiom is fixed and active: ✗ notice was sat up and taken.
entries.see also: sit back, sit around, stand up

entries.meaning: Have sex with a lot of different people.
examples: There were rumors that he slept around.
She doesn't much care who sleeps around and who doesn't.
Half the plot turns on who has been sleeping around with whom.
He slept around for a couple of years and then settled down.
They accused him of sleeping around, which he denied.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.register: informal — disapproving; it is a judgment, not a neutral description
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and habitual: the progressive is normal in the gossip it lives in — who has been sleeping around with whom.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the partner is not an object here: ✗ half the office was slept around.
entries.see also: sleep with, sleep over

entries.meaning: Stay in bed later than usual on purpose — doing it by accident is oversleeping.
examples: I slept in until eleven on Saturday.
The kids are at their grandmother's, so we can sleep in.
He never sleeps in, even on vacation.
Sleep in tomorrow — you've earned it.
She slept in and missed the first train, which is oversleeping, not sleeping in.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: staying in bed later on purpose. Progressive works — the kids are sleeping in for once.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, with no object at all: ✗ Saturday was slept in.
entries.see also: sleep over, sleep off, sleep through

entries.meaning: Get rid of the effects of drink, jet lag, or a rough night by sleeping.
examples: He's upstairs sleeping it off.
Sleep off the jet lag before you try to do any work.
She slept the whole thing off and woke up fine.
They let him sleep it off in the back office.
You can't sleep off that kind of tired in one night.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must split: sleep it off. Both orders work with a noun: sleep off the jet lag or sleep the jet lag off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: getting rid of drink, jet lag, or exhaustion by sleeping. Progressive is the usual form — he's upstairs sleeping it off.
entries.passive: restricted — the object is nearly always it, and the passive is rare and clumsy: ?the jet lag was slept off in one afternoon. Keep it active.
entries.see also: shake off, sleep in, sleep through

entries.meaning: Put a decision off until the next morning, on the theory that it will look different.
examples: Don't answer now — sleep on it.
I slept on it and changed my mind.
Let's sleep on the offer and talk tomorrow.
She wanted an answer that night; I asked to sleep on it.
Every big decision in that family gets slept on first.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: отложить решение до утра, переспать с мыслью
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition and is nearly always it: sleep on it. ✗ sleep it on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: deliberately putting a decision off overnight. Progressive is unusual because the act is a single decision — I'll sleep on it rather than ?I'm sleeping on it.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry ends on one — every big decision in that family gets slept on first; the offer was slept on and answered in the morning.
entries.see also: set aside, sit on, sleep in

entries.meaning: Spend the night at someone else's house; the noun sleepover is what children call it.
examples: Can Maddie sleep over on Friday?
He slept over at his cousin's.
Four kids slept over and nobody slept.
She asked if she could sleep over instead of driving home.
They used to sleep over every weekend one summer.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: spending the night at someone else's house. Progressive is fine — four kids are sleeping over on Friday.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the house is not an object: ✗ his cousin's was slept over.
entries.see also: sleep in, sleep around, stick around

entries.meaning: Stay asleep while something noisy is going on.
examples: He slept through the alarm and two phone calls.
She slept through the entire flight.
The baby finally slept through the night.
I slept through it — I didn't hear a thing.
Somehow all four of them slept through the storm.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: slept through the alarm, slept through it. ✗ slept it through.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though what it reports is a failure to wake: the baby finally slept through the night.
entries.passive: restricted — marginal and rare: ?the alarm was slept through again. The five entry examples are all active, and that is the natural form.
entries.see also: sleep in, sit through, sleep off

entries.meaning: Have sex with someone.
examples: They'd been sleeping with each other for months before anyone noticed.
She's not sleeping with anyone at the office.
He slept with her best friend, which ended things.
Whether he slept with her is not really the point of the story.
In the movie she sleeps with the wrong man and the plot follows from there.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the person follows the preposition: sleep with someone, sleep with him. ✗ sleep him with.
entries.register: everyday — the standard polite euphemism in American English
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: the standard American euphemism for having sex with someone. Progressive is normal — she's not sleeping with anyone at the office.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ her best friend was slept with by him. Reverse the subjects instead.
entries.see also: sleep around, sleep over

entries.meaning: Say something on someone else's behalf — and, in two fixed phrases, need no explaining or be already claimed.
examples: I can't speak for the whole department.
She speaks for the family now.
Speak for yourself — I had a great time.
His record speaks for itself.
That chair is spoken for.
The last two puppies are already spoken for.

senses.head: Talk on someone's behalf
body: You are authorized, or you are claiming to be. Speak for yourself is the standard retort to someone who claimed to. (говорить от имени)
examples: I can't speak for the whole department.
She speaks for the family now.
Speak for yourself — I had a great time.

senses.head: speak for itself — need no explanation
body: Of evidence, a record, a result. (говорить само за себя)
examples: His record speaks for itself.

senses.head: be spoken for — already claimed
body: Passive only, of a seat, a puppy, or a person who is not available. (быть занятым, зарезервированным)
examples: That chair is spoken for.
The last two puppies are already spoken for.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: говорить от имени; говорить само за себя; быть занятым (spoken for)
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: speak for the family, speak for them. ✗ speak the family for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the on-behalf sense (she's speaking for the family tonight). The two fixed phrases are stative: his record speaks for itself and be spoken for report a standing state, not an act — ✗ that chair is being spoken for.
entries.passive: restricted — the only live passive is the fixed be spoken for, and it has its own meaning: the last two puppies are already spoken for. That blocks the literal one — the family is spoken for by her reads as 'claimed', not 'represented'.
entries.see also: speak up for, stand up for, stand for

entries.meaning: Say in public what you think, especially against something powerful, and at some cost to yourself.
examples: She was the first to speak out.
He spoke out against the layoffs and lost his job three weeks later.
More people are speaking out now that the first ones did.
It took years before anyone spoke out publicly.
They warned her not to speak out.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object; what you oppose follows against.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: saying in public what you think, usually against something. Progressive is normal — more people are speaking out now.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; what you oppose follows against and will not promote: ✗ the layoffs were spoken out against by him is not usable American English.
entries.see also: speak up, speak up for, stand up for

entries.meaning: Address a subject, have a word with someone about their behavior, or resonate with a person.
examples: Can you speak to the safety question?
The report doesn't speak to costs at all.
I'll speak to him about the noise.
The book spoke to me in a way nothing else had.
That kind of music speaks to a lot of people.

senses.head: Address a topic
body: Formal American usage, common in meetings and reports: the speaker deals with that question specifically. (затрагивать вопрос, говорить о)
examples: Can you speak to the safety question?
The report doesn't speak to costs at all.

senses.head: Have a word with someone
body: A quiet euphemism for a reprimand. (поговорить с, сделать внушение)
examples: I'll speak to him about the noise.

senses.head: Resonate with someone
body: The subject is a book, a song, or an idea, and the object is the person it reaches. (находить отклик у)
examples: The book spoke to me in a way nothing else had.
That kind of music speaks to a lot of people.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: затрагивать (вопрос), говорить о; сделать внушение; находить отклик
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: speak to the question, speak to it. ✗ speak the question to.
entries.register: everyday; the 'address a topic' sense is formal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the address-a-topic sense (can you speak to the safety question?) and the reprimand sense (I'll speak to him about the noise). The resonate sense is closer to stative — that music speaks to a lot of people — though the progressive is heard: this song is really speaking to me.
entries.passive: restricted — the reprimand sense passivizes freely: he was spoken to about the noise. The topic sense is marginal (?the safety question was never spoken to) and the resonate sense refuses: ✗ I was spoken to by the book.
entries.see also: speak for, set forth, speak up

entries.meaning: Talk louder, or say the thing that needs saying.
examples: Speak up — we can't hear you in the back.
He asked her to speak up twice.
If something's wrong, speak up.
Nobody spoke up at the meeting.
She spoke up when it counted.

senses.head: Talk louder
body: Literal, and the most common use in a room. (говорить громче)
examples: Speak up — we can't hear you in the back.
He asked her to speak up twice.

senses.head: Say what you think
body: Smaller and more personal than speak out: you break a silence in the room you are in. (высказаться, подать голос)
examples: If something's wrong, speak up.
Nobody spoke up at the meeting.
She spoke up when it counted.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: talking louder and saying the thing that needs saying. Progressive is fine — nobody was speaking up.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, with no object in either sense: ✗ the problem was spoken up.
entries.see also: speak out, speak up for, sing out

entries.meaning: Say something publicly in support of someone or something.
examples: Two coworkers spoke up for him at the hearing.
Somebody has to speak up for the people who can't.
She spoke up for me when it would have been easier not to.
Nobody spoke up for the proposal, so it quietly died.
He never speaks up for himself.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: speak up for the new guy, speak up for him. ✗ speak the new guy up for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: publicly backing a person or a proposal. Progressive works — he was speaking up for her before anyone else would.
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part passive is grammatical but stiff: ?he was spoken up for at the hearing. American usage prefers the active, or be stood up for.
entries.see also: stand up for, stick up for, speak out

entries.meaning: Go faster, or make something go faster. The past is usually sped up; speeded up is also heard, mostly of processes rather than vehicles.
examples: The line sped up once they opened a second register.
Can we speed the process up a little?
Speed it up — we're losing the light.
New software sped up the whole review.
He sped up on the straightaway and nearly missed the turn.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — speed up the process or speed the process up; with a pronoun it must split: speed it up. With no object it simply means going faster: the car sped up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event either way — the line sped up (no agent) or new software sped up the review (agent named).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the whole review was sped up by new software; the process has been sped up considerably. No passive of the intransitive the car sped up.
entries.see also: set back, shoot up, spin out

entries.meaning: Separate part of a company or a series into something of its own.
examples: They spun off the research division.
The board spun the chemicals unit off into a company of its own.
The parent company spun it off in 2019.
Two labs were spun off and later merged.
The sitcom spun off two other series.
A whole podcast spun off from one episode.

senses.head: Make part of a company into a separate one
body: Corporate: the parent keeps some of it or none of it, but the new firm stands alone. (выделить в отдельную компанию)
examples: They spun off the research division.
The board spun the chemicals unit off into a company of its own.
The parent company spun it off in 2019.
Two labs were spun off and later merged.

senses.head: Produce a derivative show or product
body: The noun spin-off is commoner than the verb here. (породить ответвление)
examples: The sitcom spun off two other series.
A whole podcast spun off from one episode.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: выделить (подразделение) в отдельную компанию; породить ответвление
entries.separable: yes — spin off the research division or spin the research division off; with a pronoun it must split: spun it off.
entries.transitive: either — usually transitive; a show or a company can also spin off from something with no object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: separating part of a company, and producing a derivative show. The television sense also runs agentlessly — a whole podcast spun off from one episode.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense, and the entry uses it — two labs were spun off and later merged; the chemicals unit was spun off into a company of its own. No passive of the intransitive a podcast spun off from one episode.
entries.see also: split off, set up, sell off

entries.meaning: Lose control of a car in a spin — or stretch something out far longer than it needs to be.
examples: The truck spun out on black ice.
She spun out and ended up facing the wrong way.
He spun out the story for another twenty minutes.
They spun the negotiation out until the deadline.
Don't spin it out — just tell us.

senses.head: Lose control of a vehicle
body: American, and the standard word for it on the road and in racing. No object. (занести, потерять управление)
examples: The truck spun out on black ice.
She spun out and ended up facing the wrong way.

senses.head: Make something last longer than it should
body: Of a story, a negotiation, a supply of money. (растянуть, затянуть)
examples: He spun out the story for another twenty minutes.
They spun the negotiation out until the deadline.
Don't spin it out — just tell us.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: занести, потерять управление (об авто); растянуть, затянуть
entries.separable: yes in the 'prolong' sense — spin out the story or spin the story out, and a pronoun splits it: spin it out. In the driving sense there is no object: the truck spun out.
entries.register: everyday in the driving sense (American); the 'prolong' sense is commoner in Britain
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: losing control of a car (no agent, no object) and stretching something out too long (he spun out the story for twenty minutes).
entries.passive: restricted — only the prolong sense passivizes: the negotiation was spun out until the deadline. The driving sense is objectless: ✗ the truck was spun out on black ice.
entries.see also: spin off, speed up

entries.meaning: Break away from a larger group, or break a piece off one.
examples: A faction split off and started its own party.
They split the shipping business off last year.
One climber split off from the group at the ridge.
The company split off its two smallest units.
It was easier to split it off than to fix it.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — split off the shipping business or split the shipping business off, and a pronoun splits it: split it off. With no object it is the group itself that separates: a faction split off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the group separates itself (a faction split off) or somebody separates a piece (they split the shipping business off).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the shipping business was split off last year; the two smallest units were split off. No passive of a faction split off.
entries.see also: split up, spin off

entries.meaning: Tell someone in authority what another person did.
examples: Somebody split on us.
He wouldn't split on his mates.
She was afraid her brother would split on her.
They found out because a neighbor split on them.
Nobody in that class ever split on anybody.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: split on his friends, split on them. ✗ split his friends on.
entries.register: British — informal; an American says rat on, snitch on, or tell on
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: telling authority what someone else did. Progressive is fine — he thought his brother was splitting on him.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but rare, and British where the verb is: ?they were split on by a neighbor. Americans would say they got ratted on.
entries.see also: stand by, stick together, sell out

entries.meaning: End a relationship — or divide something, or a group, into parts.
examples: They split up after six years.
She split up with him in April.
Let's split up the work before anybody starts.
We split the class up into pairs.
Split it up four ways.

senses.head: End a relationship
body: No object; the other person follows with. (расстаться, разойтись)
examples: They split up after six years.
She split up with him in April.

senses.head: Divide into parts or groups
body: Transitive and separable, of money, work, or a class. (разделить, поделить)
examples: Let's split up the work before anybody starts.
We split the class up into pairs.
Split it up four ways.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — split up the money or split the money up, and a pronoun splits it: split it up. When a couple splits up there is no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: a relationship ending (no object) and dividing something or someone into parts (we split the class up into pairs).
entries.passive: yes in the divide sense — the work was split up before anybody started; the class was split up into pairs. Not in the relationship sense: they were split up after six years reads as somebody else separating them, not as the couple's own breakup.
entries.see also: split off, sell off, spread out

entries.meaning: Move apart to cover more ground, open something out flat, or stretch payments over time.
examples: The search party spread out along the riverbank.
Spread out — you're all standing in the same three feet.
He spread the map out on the hood of the truck.
She spread out a blanket under the tree.
Spread it out so we can all see.
You can spread the payments out over a year.

senses.head: Move apart to cover more ground
body: No object; of a search party, a crowd, a line of hikers. (рассредоточиться)
examples: The search party spread out along the riverbank.
Spread out — you're all standing in the same three feet.

senses.head: Open something out flat
body: Of a map, a blanket, a set of photographs. (разложить, расстелить)
examples: He spread the map out on the hood of the truck.
She spread out a blanket under the tree.
Spread it out so we can all see.

senses.head: Distribute over time
body: Of payments, work, or appointments. (растянуть по времени)
examples: You can spread the payments out over a year.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — spread out the map or spread the map out, and a pronoun splits it: spread it out. When people spread out over an area there is no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: people moving apart (no object), opening something out flat, and distributing payments over time.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the map was spread out on the hood of the truck; the payments can be spread out over a year. No passive of the disperse sense: ✗ the riverbank was spread out along.
entries.see also: shake out, set out, split up

entries.meaning: Pay for something as a treat, usually for other people; the past is sprang for (or sprung for in speech).
examples: I'll spring for dinner.
He sprang for the good seats.
Nobody wanted to spring for a cab, so we walked.
She sprang for it because it was his birthday.
If you spring for the coffee, I'll bring the doughnuts.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: spring for dinner, spring for it. ✗ spring dinner for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: paying for something as a treat. A single act, so the progressive is unusual — I'll spring for dinner rather than ?I'm springing for dinner.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ dinner was sprung for by him, ✗ the good seats were sprung for. Keep it active.
entries.see also: shoot for, spring on

entries.meaning: Tell someone something surprising with no warning at all.
examples: Don't spring the news on her at dinner.
He sprang it on me an hour before the flight.
They sprang a surprise inspection on the whole department.
She sprang the question on him in front of everyone.
Nobody likes having a deadline sprung on them.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress and on is reduced — SPRANG it on me
entries.separable: the thing you spring always sits between the verb and on, and the person comes after it: spring the news on her, spring it on me. ✗ spring on me the news.
entries.transitive: yes — two objects: spring something on someone
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and punctual: a single unannounced act. Progressive fine for the scheduled kind: they're springing a new policy on us Monday.
entries.passive: yes, on the thing sprung, and common in the -ing form: a surprise inspection was sprung on the whole department, nobody likes having a deadline sprung on them. The person after on cannot become subject: ✗ she was sprung the news on.
entries.see also: spring up, spring for, shake up

entries.meaning: Appear suddenly, and usually in numbers.
examples: Coffee shops sprang up all over the neighborhood.
A rumor sprang up that the store was closing.
Tents sprang up in the park overnight.
New competitors spring up every year.
A breeze sprang up just after sunset.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an event of sudden appearance, usually in numbers. Progressive normal: coffee shops are springing up all over the neighborhood.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive — there is no object to promote: ✗ tents were sprung up in the park. For an agent, switch verbs: they pitched tents in the park overnight.
entries.see also: set in, shoot up, spread out

entries.meaning: Stand in one place doing nothing useful, usually while waiting.
examples: Twenty people stood around waiting for somebody to open the door.
Don't stand around out there in the cold.
They stood around the grill talking about nothing in particular.
He stands around all shift and still gets paid.
We stood around for an hour before anyone told us anything.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity verb of idling; the progressive is its home tense: twenty people were standing around waiting.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive: ✗ the door was stood around by twenty people. Any place phrase (stood around the grill) is an adjunct, not an object.
entries.see also: sit around, stand back, stand by

entries.meaning: Move out of the way — physically, or by giving up a position to someone else.
examples: Stand aside and let them through.
The crowd stood aside for the stretcher.
He stood aside and let his deputy run the campaign.
She refuses to stand aside.
Two board members stood aside rather than fight about it.

senses.head: Move out of the way
body: Literal, and often an instruction. (посторониться, отойти в сторону)
examples: Stand aside and let them through.
The crowd stood aside for the stretcher.

senses.head: Step down so someone else can take over
body: Figurative: you could have kept the job and chose not to. (уступить место)
examples: He stood aside and let his deputy run the campaign.
She refuses to stand aside.
Two board members stood aside rather than fight about it.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: посторониться, отойти в сторону; уступить место
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the physical stepping out of the way (the crowd stood aside) and the figurative giving up of a post (he stood aside and let his deputy run it).
entries.passive: no. Intransitive in both senses: ✗ the stretcher was stood aside for. The deputy sense needs a different verb for a passive: the campaign was handed to his deputy.
entries.see also: stand back, stand down

entries.meaning: Move away from something — or step back mentally and look at the whole of it.
examples: Stand back — the door swings out.
Everyone stood back when the truck started rolling.
Stand back and look at the whole page.
It helps to stand back for a week before you decide.
If you stand back from it, the pattern is obvious.

senses.head: Move away from something
body: Literal, usually for safety. (отойти назад)
examples: Stand back — the door swings out.
Everyone stood back when the truck started rolling.

senses.head: Take a detached view
body: You stop working on the detail in order to see the shape of the thing. (взглянуть со стороны)
examples: Stand back and look at the whole page.
It helps to stand back for a week before you decide.
If you stand back from it, the pattern is obvious.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the literal sense (everyone stood back when the truck started rolling) and in the detached-view sense, where it is a deliberate mental act: stand back and look at the whole page.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive in both senses: ✗ the truck was stood back from. Say the crowd was moved back if you need an agent.
entries.see also: stand aside, sit back, stand by

entries.meaning: Stay loyal to a person or a statement, wait ready for orders, or watch something happen without acting.
examples: She stood by him through the whole trial.
I stand by every word of it.
They stood by the original estimate.
Crews are standing by.
Stand by for an announcement.
We can't just stand by and watch it happen.

senses.head: Support someone, or keep to something
body: Of people you refuse to abandon and of statements you refuse to retract. (поддерживать; не отступать от)
examples: She stood by him through the whole trial.
I stand by every word of it.
They stood by the original estimate.

senses.head: Wait in readiness
body: No object; the source of standby. (быть наготове)
examples: Crews are standing by.
Stand by for an announcement.

senses.head: Do nothing while something bad happens
body: Always a reproach, and usually with and watch. (стоять сложа руки)
examples: We can't just stand by and watch it happen.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: поддерживать, не бросать; не отступать от (решения); быть наготове; стоять сложа руки
entries.separable: no in every sense — the object always follows the whole phrase: stand by your decision, stand by her. ✗ stand your decision by, ✗ stand her by. In the 'wait' and 'do nothing' senses there is no object at all.
entries.verb type: stative in the loyalty sense — a continuing stance, not an act: I stand by every word of it, and the progressive is odd for a statement (?I'm standing by my estimate) though normal of a person (she was standing by him through all of it). Action — dynamic in the readiness sense (crews are standing by) and the do-nothing reproach (we can't just stand by and watch).
entries.passive: no. The loyalty sense is a prepositional verb that refuses promotion: ✗ he was stood by by his friends; senses 2 and 3 take no object at all: ✗ an announcement was stood by for.
entries.see also: stick by, stand up for, sit back

entries.meaning: Withdraw — from a post, from a confrontation, or from a state of alert.
examples: He stood down as chairman in June.
She was asked to stand down and refused.
Tell them to stand down — it's handled.
The unit stood down at midnight.
Crews stood down once the fire was contained.

senses.head: Withdraw, resign, or back off
body: Of a chairman giving up the job, a candidate quitting a race, or a person told to drop a fight. (уйти с поста, снять кандидатуру; отступить)
examples: He stood down as chairman in June.
She was asked to stand down and refused.
Tell them to stand down — it's handled.

senses.head: Come off alert
body: Military and emergency-services vocabulary. (отбой)
examples: The unit stood down at midnight.
Crews stood down once the fire was contained.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отступить, снять кандидатуру, уйти с поста; отбой (воен.)
entries.separable: no object in ordinary use, so nothing goes inside it. The military transitive stand the crews down exists but is rare.
entries.register: everyday — but note the split: Americans say step down for resigning and reserve stand down for military, police, and 'back off' uses, where the British use it for resigning too
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the resigning or backing off (he stood down as chairman in June) and the coming off alert (the unit stood down at midnight).
entries.passive: restricted. No passive from ordinary intransitive use: ✗ the chairmanship was stood down. Only the rare military transitive gives one — the crews were stood down once the fire was contained — and even that is reporters' and briefers' English.
entries.see also: stand aside, stand back, shut down

entries.meaning: Be short for something, put up with something, or represent a principle.
examples: What does NPR stand for?
The R stands for Rachel.
I won't stand for it.
No teacher there would stand for that kind of talk.
The flag stands for something to her.
It isn't clear what the party stands for anymore.
She's standing for Parliament in the spring.

senses.head: Be an abbreviation of
body: The most literal sense, and the one children learn first. (означать, расшифровываться как)
examples: What does NPR stand for?
The R stands for Rachel.

senses.head: Tolerate
body: Negative only: I won't stand for it is idiomatic, but ✗ I stand for it is not English. (терпеть, мириться с)
examples: I won't stand for it.
No teacher there would stand for that kind of talk.

senses.head: Represent a principle
body: Of a flag, a party, a person's reputation. (отстаивать, символизировать)
examples: The flag stands for something to her.
It isn't clear what the party stands for anymore.

senses.head: Run for office
body: British only: an American candidate runs for office. (баллотироваться)
examples: She's standing for Parliament in the spring.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: означать, расшифровываться как; терпеть, мириться с; отстаивать; баллотироваться (брит.)
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: stand for freedom, stand for it. ✗ stand freedom for, and never ✗ stand it for.
entries.verb type: stative in the core senses — being an abbreviation of (the R stands for Rachel) and representing a principle (it isn't clear what the party stands for); both reject the progressive: ✗ NPR is standing for something. The tolerate sense is stative too, and negative-only: I won't stand for it, ✗ I stand for it. Only the British run-for-office sense is dynamic: she's standing for Parliament in the spring.
entries.passive: no. Stative and prepositional: ✗ Rachel is stood for by the R, ✗ something is stood for by the flag. The tolerate sense is marginally attested in stiff writing (that kind of talk will not be stood for here), but no American says it.
entries.see also: speak for, stand up for, stand up to

entries.meaning: Take someone's place for a while; the noun stand-in is the person who does it.
examples: Her deputy stood in while she was away.
Can you stand in tonight?
He's only standing in until they hire somebody.
A stand-in read the part at the rehearsal.
Nobody wanted to stand in on that little notice.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object; the person you replace follows for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a temporary activity; the progressive is normal and often the point: he's only standing in until they hire somebody.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive — the person replaced follows for, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ she was stood in while she was away.
entries.see also: stand in for, sit in for, sit in

entries.meaning: Take the place of someone or something else, temporarily or symbolically.
examples: I'm standing in for Dana this week.
A cardboard cutout stood in for the actor in the wide shots.
Who's standing in for him at the hearing?
She stood in for her sister at the ceremony.
The number stands in for a name nobody ever learned.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: stand in for the host, stand in for her. ✗ stand the host in for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, whether of a person covering a shift (I'm standing in for Dana this week) or a thing standing symbolically for another (the number stands in for a name), where it edges toward stative.
entries.passive: no. A three-part verb whose object stays put: ✗ Dana was stood in for by me, ✗ the actor was stood in for by a cardboard cutout. Say a cutout replaced the actor.
entries.see also: stand in, sit in for, speak for

entries.meaning: Be impossible to miss — because you look different, or because you are better.
examples: A red door stands out on that street.
He stood out in a room full of dark suits.
Two applicants stood out.
What stands out is the writing.
It's a good album, but nothing on it really stands out.

senses.head: Be conspicuous
body: Neutral: it is simply easy to see. (выделяться, бросаться в глаза)
examples: A red door stands out on that street.
He stood out in a room full of dark suits.

senses.head: Be clearly better
body: The compliment sense, and the source of the noun standout. (быть на голову выше)
examples: Two applicants stood out.
What stands out is the writing.
It's a good album, but nothing on it really stands out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: выделяться, бросаться в глаза; быть на голову выше
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: stative in both senses — being conspicuous (a red door stands out on that street) and being clearly better (two applicants stood out). It resists the progressive: ✗ a red door is standing out on that street; the office-speak what's standing out to me is the exception, not the rule.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive, and stative besides: ✗ a room full of dark suits was stood out in. Use set apart for an agent: the writing sets the album apart.
entries.see also: set apart, shine through, show off

entries.meaning: Get to your feet, leave someone waiting at a date you never came to, or hold up under examination.
examples: Everyone stood up when she came in.
Stand up so I can see the hem.
He stood her up twice.
She stood her date up and never even texted.
I got stood up at a very nice restaurant.
That story won't stand up in court.
The fabric stands up to a lot of washing.

senses.head: Rise to your feet
body: No object; the literal sense. (встать)
examples: Everyone stood up when she came in.
Stand up so I can see the hem.

senses.head: Fail to keep a date
body: Transitive, and the person always sits in the middle. (продинамить, не прийти на свидание)
examples: He stood her up twice.
She stood her date up and never even texted.
I got stood up at a very nice restaurant.

senses.head: Survive testing or scrutiny
body: Of evidence, an argument, or material under wear; often with to. (выдержать проверку)
examples: That story won't stand up in court.
The fabric stands up to a lot of washing.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: встать; продинамить, не прийти на свидание; выдержать проверку
entries.separable: yes in the 'fail to show up' sense, where the person must sit inside: he stood me up, she stood him up. ✗ stood up me. The 'rise' and 'survive scrutiny' senses take no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the rise sense (everyone stood up when she came in) and the jilting sense (he stood her up twice). The survive-scrutiny sense is stative, a disposition rather than an event: that story won't stand up in court, ✗ the fabric is standing up to a lot of washing.
entries.passive: yes in the jilting sense only, and get is as common as be: I got stood up at a very nice restaurant. The other two senses are intransitive: ✗ court was stood up in by that story.
entries.see also: stand up for, stand up to, show up

entries.meaning: Defend a person or a principle openly, usually at some cost.
examples: Stand up for yourself.
She stood up for the new guy when nobody else would.
You have to stand up for what you believe.
He never stood up for us once.
Somebody stood up for her in that meeting, and it mattered.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: stand up for the new guy, stand up for him. ✗ stand the new guy up for, which would say something else entirely.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of open defense, usually costly and usually at a moment you can point to: she stood up for the new guy when nobody else would.
entries.passive: no. The three-part verb will not promote its object, and the string collides with the jilting sense of stand up: ✗ the new guy was stood up for by her reads wrong twice over. Say she defended him.
entries.see also: stick up for, speak up for, stand up to

entries.meaning: Face down someone stronger than you — or, of a thing, survive hard use.
examples: She was the first person there to stand up to him.
It takes something to stand up to a room like that.
These boots stand up to a New England winter.
The old bridge stood up to the flood.
Cheap paint doesn't stand up to sun.

senses.head: Confront someone powerful
body: The person you confront has the advantage; that is what makes it standing up to them. (дать отпор, противостоять)
examples: She was the first person there to stand up to him.
It takes something to stand up to a room like that.

senses.head: Withstand hard use
body: Of boots, paint, bridges, arguments. (выдерживать)
examples: These boots stand up to a New England winter.
The old bridge stood up to the flood.
Cheap paint doesn't stand up to sun.

entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: stand up to the boss, stand up to him. ✗ stand the boss up to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the confrontation sense (she was the first person there to stand up to him); stative in the withstand sense, which states a property of the thing: these boots stand up to a New England winter, ✗ cheap paint is standing up to sun.
entries.passive: no. Neither sense promotes its object: ✗ he was stood up to by her, ✗ a New England winter is stood up to by these boots. Use withstand — the flood was withstood by the old bridge — or better, keep it active.
entries.see also: stand up for, stand up, strike back

entries.meaning: Leave quietly enough that nobody notices you going.
examples: They stole away before the speeches started.
He stole away from the party around ten.
We stole away for an hour and nobody missed us.
She stole him away from the conversation for a minute.
The band stole the crowd away from the main stage.
The two of them stole away down the back stairs.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: usually there is no object — you steal away yourself. When it does take one, the object sits inside: stole her away from the conversation.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a quiet act of leaving (they stole away before the speeches started) or, transitively, of drawing someone off (she stole him away from the conversation).
entries.passive: restricted. Only the transitive use passivizes, and it stays literary: the crowd was stolen away from the main stage. The ordinary reflexive use has no passive: ✗ the party was stolen away from by him, and he was stolen away invites the kidnapping reading.
entries.see also: steal up on, stick around

entries.meaning: Come up close to someone or something without being heard — used of hunters, and of time.
examples: He stole up on the deer from downwind.
Don't steal up on me like that.
Winter steals up on you out here.
The photographer stole up on them and got the shot of the trip.
Forty stole up on him faster than he expected.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: steal up on the deer, steal up on them. ✗ steal the deer up on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of hunters and of time alike: he stole up on the deer from downwind, winter steals up on you out here. Progressive fine: don't look now, but forty is stealing up on him.
entries.passive: no. A three-part verb that will not promote its object, and the participle drags in the theft sense: ✗ the deer was stolen up on. Say he crept up on the deer.
entries.see also: steal away, spring on

entries.meaning: Stay where you are a while longer instead of leaving.
examples: Stick around — she'll be back in ten minutes.
He stuck around after the show to help clean up.
Most of them didn't stick around for a second year.
I'd stick around if there were anywhere to sit.
Stick around long enough and you'll see it happen twice.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity of staying put; common as a bare imperative and in the progressive: stick around, he's sticking around for another year.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive: ✗ the show was stuck around after. Time and purpose phrases (stick around for a second year) are adjuncts, not objects.
entries.see also: stick with, sit around, stick together

entries.meaning: Keep working at something difficult without giving up.
examples: Stick at it and you'll get there.
She stuck at the piano for six years.
He never could stick at anything for long.
If you stick at it, the hard part passes.
They told him to stick at it another term.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: stick at it, stick at the piano. ✗ stick it at.
entries.register: British — an American says stick with it or keep at it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity of persisting over time; British. Progressive normal: she's sticking at it another term.
entries.passive: no. A prepositional verb whose object stays after the preposition, and stuck pulls in the 'jammed' reading: ✗ the piano was stuck at for six years. American English sidesteps it entirely with stick with or keep at.
entries.see also: stick with, stick to, stick out

entries.meaning: Stay loyal to a person, or keep to a decision, when walking away would be easier.
examples: His friends stuck by him.
She stuck by her story through an hour of questioning.
They stuck by the plan even after the money ran out.
You stick by your people; that's the whole rule.
Not many stuck by him after that.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: не бросать, остаться верным; не отступать от
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: stick by your friends, stick by him. ✗ stick him by.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though it names a stance held over time rather than a single act: his friends stuck by him, they're sticking by the plan even after the money ran out.
entries.passive: no. The object never leaves the preposition, and the passive would be read as glue or as being trapped: ✗ he was stuck by his friends. Say his friends supported him.
entries.see also: stand by, stick with, stick together

entries.meaning: Poke out from a surface, be impossible to miss, or hang on to the end of something unpleasant.
examples: A nail was sticking out of the board.
Don't stick your elbow out the window.
He sticks out like a sore thumb in that jacket.
It's a miserable job, but I'm going to stick it out.
She stuck out the whole season on a bad knee.

senses.head: Protrude
body: No object when the thing itself sticks out; an object when you push something out. (торчать, высовываться)
examples: A nail was sticking out of the board.
Don't stick your elbow out the window.

senses.head: Be conspicuous
body: Usually in the fixed simile stick out like a sore thumb. (выделяться, бросаться в глаза)
examples: He sticks out like a sore thumb in that jacket.

senses.head: Endure to the end
body: Always in the split form stick it out. (вытерпеть, дотянуть)
examples: It's a miserable job, but I'm going to stick it out.
She stuck out the whole season on a bad knee.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: торчать, высовываться; выделяться; вытерпеть до конца
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — stick out your tongue or stick your tongue out, and a pronoun splits it: stick it out. Note that stick it out is also the fixed way to say 'endure to the end'. With no object it simply means protrude.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when you push something out (don't stick your elbow out the window) and when you endure to the end (I'm going to stick it out). The intransitive protrude sense is a state of position, though the progressive is normal for it: a nail was sticking out of the board. The conspicuous sense is stative: he sticks out like a sore thumb.
entries.passive: no in practice. The protrude sense is intransitive; the transitive uses give bad passives that collide with stuck 'jammed': ✗ her tongue was stuck out, ✗ the whole season was stuck out on a bad knee.
entries.see also: stand out, sit out, stick with

entries.meaning: Keep to a plan, a rule, a subject, or a position instead of wandering off it.
examples: Stick to the plan.
Let's stick to the facts.
He sticks to the speed limit, which is more than I can say.
She stuck to her guns and won.
I'm sticking to water tonight.

senses.head: Keep to a plan or a subject
body: The core sense: no improvising, no digressions. (придерживаться)
examples: Stick to the plan.
Let's stick to the facts.
He sticks to the speed limit, which is more than I can say.

senses.head: stick to your guns — refuse to back down
body: A fixed phrase, and always approving. (стоять на своём)
examples: She stuck to her guns and won.

senses.head: Use or consume nothing else
body: Of drinks, foods, and brands. (ограничиться чем-л.)
examples: I'm sticking to water tonight.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: stick to the plan, stick to it. ✗ stick the plan to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an ongoing choice not to stray: stick to the plan, I'm sticking to water tonight, he sticks to the speed limit.
entries.passive: restricted. Formal writing allows it — the timetable was stuck to throughout — but the glue reading makes speakers avoid it, and ✗ her guns were stuck to is impossible because the object is part of a fixed phrase.
entries.see also: stick with, stick at, stand by

entries.meaning: Stay loyal to one another as a group, especially under pressure.
examples: Families stick together.
If we stick together, they can't pick us off one at a time.
That crew stuck together for thirty years.
They stuck together through two bad winters and a lawsuit.
Stick together and nobody gets lost.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: держаться вместе, стоять друг за друга
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a group activity sustained over time: families stick together, that crew stuck together for thirty years.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive with a plural or collective subject: ✗ they were stuck together by the crew would say the glue thing instead.
entries.see also: stick by, stand by, split up

entries.meaning: Point upward, put something up on a surface, or rob a place at gunpoint.
examples: His hair sticks up no matter what he does to it.
A few reeds stuck up through the ice.
Stick the notice up by the door.
She stuck it up on the fridge.
Two men stuck up the liquor store on Tenth.

senses.head: Point upward
body: No object. (торчать вверх)
examples: His hair sticks up no matter what he does to it.
A few reeds stuck up through the ice.

senses.head: Put something up on a wall
body: Transitive and separable. (повесить, приклеить)
examples: Stick the notice up by the door.
She stuck it up on the fridge.

senses.head: Rob at gunpoint
body: Informal and dated-sounding; stick 'em up is the movie line. (ограбить под дулом)
examples: Two men stuck up the liquor store on Tenth.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: торчать вверх; повесить, приклеить; ограбить (под дулом)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — stick up a poster or stick a poster up, and a pronoun splits it: stick it up. With no object it means point upward.
entries.register: everyday in the 'protrude' and 'put up' senses; informal in the robbery sense, where the noun stick-up is commoner than the verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the put-up sense (stick the notice up by the door) and the robbery sense (two men stuck up the liquor store). The protrude sense is a state of position, though the progressive is fine: his hair is sticking up again.
entries.passive: yes in the two transitive senses: the notice was stuck up by the door, the liquor store on Tenth was stuck up by two men — the robbery passive sounds as dated as the active. No passive from the protrude sense: ✗ the ice was stuck up through.
entries.see also: stick out, stick up for, shake down

entries.meaning: Defend someone who is being criticized or picked on.
examples: Her brother always stuck up for her.
Somebody has to stick up for the kid.
Stick up for yourself for once.
He stuck up for me in front of the whole crew.
Nobody stuck up for him, which told you exactly where he stood.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress; the last word is reduced
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split: stick up for your friends, stick up for her. ✗ stick your friends up for.
entries.register: informal — the spoken everyday version of stand up for
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of defending someone under fire: her brother always stuck up for her, somebody has to stick up for the kid.
entries.passive: no. Three-part verbs do not promote their objects, and stuck misreads: ✗ the kid was stuck up for by somebody. Say somebody defended the kid.
entries.see also: stand up for, speak up for, stick by

entries.meaning: Keep at something, stay close to someone, or — with the memory as subject — refuse to leave a person's head.
examples: Stick with it — the second week is easier.
We stuck with the old system for another year.
Stick with me and you won't get lost.
That image stuck with me for years.
Her advice has stuck with him ever since.

senses.head: Keep at something, keep using something
body: The American answer to British stick at. (не бросать, продолжать)
examples: Stick with it — the second week is easier.
We stuck with the old system for another year.

senses.head: Stay close to someone
body: Physical, and usually an instruction. (держаться рядом с)
examples: Stick with me and you won't get lost.

senses.head: Stay in someone's memory
body: Here the thing remembered is the subject and the person is the object. (запомниться, засесть в памяти)
examples: That image stuck with me for years.
Her advice has stuck with him ever since.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.русский: не бросать, продолжать; держаться рядом; запомниться
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: stick with it, stick with the old system. ✗ stick it with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the persist and stay-close senses (stick with it, stick with me and you won't get lost). The memory sense is stative — the thing remembered is the subject and simply stays there: that image stuck with me for years.
entries.passive: no. The object stays after the preposition: ✗ the old system was stuck with for another year. Note that be stuck with does exist — I'm stuck with the bill — but that is a different verb meaning 'be saddled with', not the passive of this one.
entries.see also: stick to, stick at, stick around

entries.meaning: Hit back after being attacked — with fists, with words, or with a lawsuit.
examples: They struck back within the week.
She didn't strike back, which surprised everyone in the room.
The company struck back with a lawsuit.
He struck back hard in the second debate.
Wait a day before you strike back.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: nothing to separate — it takes no object; whoever you hit back at follows at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a retaliatory event: they struck back within the week, the company struck back with a lawsuit.
entries.passive: no. Intransitive — whoever you hit back at follows at: ✗ he was struck back, which would only be heard as the plain verb strike.
entries.see also: stand up to, set upon, swing at

entries.meaning: Cancel a law from the bench — or, of illness, fell someone suddenly.
examples: The court struck down the statute.
An appeals panel struck it down in April.
They struck the ordinance down on free-speech grounds.
He was struck down by a stroke at fifty-one.
The epidemic struck down thousands in a month.

senses.head: Invalidate a law
body: The standard American legal verb: a court strikes down a statute. (отменить, признать недействительным)
examples: The court struck down the statute.
An appeals panel struck it down in April.
They struck the ordinance down on free-speech grounds.

senses.head: Kill or disable suddenly
body: Usually passive, of disease or a stroke; slightly literary. (сразить, свалить)
examples: He was struck down by a stroke at fifty-one.
The epidemic struck down thousands in a month.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: отменить (закон), признать недействительным; сразить, свалить (о болезни)
entries.separable: yes — strike down the law or strike the law down; with a pronoun it must split: struck it down.
entries.register: everyday; the legal sense is formal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual in both senses, the legal invalidating (the court struck down the statute) and the sudden felling by illness (the epidemic struck down thousands in a month).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form in both senses: the statute was struck down on free-speech grounds, he was struck down by a stroke at fifty-one.
entries.see also: shoot down, set aside, strike out

entries.meaning: Remove someone's name from a professional register, ending their right to practice.
examples: He was struck off in 2011.
The board struck her off after the second complaint.
The council struck both doctors off in the same week.
Two surgeons were struck off that year.
They threatened to strike him off.
Being struck off ends the career, not just the job.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: исключить из реестра, лишить права практики
entries.separable: yes — strike off two surgeons or strike two surgeons off; with a pronoun it must split: struck him off.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object, and it is nearly always passive: was struck off
entries.register: British — an American doctor is struck from the rolls or has a license revoked, and an American lawyer is disbarred
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual, an administrative act ending a career: the board struck her off after the second complaint. British; an American license is revoked.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the default: he was struck off in 2011, two surgeons were struck off that year. The -ing form is just as common: being struck off ends the career, not just the job.
entries.see also: strike out, shut down, stand down

entries.meaning: Suddenly think of an idea or a solution.
examples: She struck on the answer in the shower.
He struck on a way to pay for the whole thing.
They struck on the idea of selling the tickets in pairs.
Nobody had struck on it before.
Late that night he struck on the phrase he had been looking for.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: strike on an idea, strike on it. ✗ strike an idea on. The variant strike upon behaves the same way.
entries.register: rare — literary; in speech Americans say hit on an idea
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual: the moment an idea arrives, not a process. ✗ she is striking on the answer. Rare and literary; Americans say hit on.
entries.passive: no. A prepositional verb whose object will not move: ✗ the answer was struck on in the shower, ✗ it had not been struck on before.
entries.see also: strike up, strike out, spring up

entries.meaning: Cross words out, get retired on three strikes, fail completely, or head off on your own.
examples: Strike out the last sentence.
The editor struck it out without asking.
She struck the whole paragraph out.
He struck out three times in a row.
The rookie struck him out on four pitches.
I struck out with that client.
She struck out on her own at nineteen.

senses.head: Cross out written words
body: Editorial and legal: the words stay visible but are cancelled. (вычеркнуть)
examples: Strike out the last sentence.
The editor struck it out without asking.
She struck the whole paragraph out.

senses.head: Baseball: three strikes
body: The batter strikes out; the pitcher strikes him out. (выбить, выбыть)
examples: He struck out three times in a row.
The rookie struck him out on four pitches.

senses.head: Fail completely
body: Informal, straight from baseball. (потерпеть неудачу, пролететь)
examples: I struck out with that client.

senses.head: Set off on your own
body: Usually strike out on your own, of a person leaving a firm or a family. (отправиться самостоятельно)
examples: She struck out on her own at nineteen.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: вычеркнуть; выбить/выбыть (бейсбол); потерпеть неудачу; отправиться самостоятельно
entries.separable: yes — strike out that line or strike that line out, and a pronoun splits it: strike it out. In baseball a pitcher strikes a batter out, but a batter simply strikes out, with no object at all.
entries.register: everyday; the baseball and 'fail' senses are American
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: crossing out words (strike out the last sentence), the baseball event either way (he struck out three times; the rookie struck him out), failing (I struck out with that client), and setting off alone (she struck out on her own at nineteen).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses: the last sentence was struck out, the whole paragraph was struck out without asking, he was struck out on four pitches. No passive from the batter's, the failing, or the setting-off senses, which take no object: ✗ that client was struck out with.
entries.see also: strike down, strike off, set out

entries.meaning: Begin a conversation, a friendship, or a piece of music.
examples: They struck up a conversation in line at the post office.
He struck up a friendship with the woman next door.
The band struck up a march and everyone stood.
She strikes up a conversation with absolutely everyone.
They struck up a correspondence that lasted forty years.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: no in practice — grammars class it as separable, but the object always follows the particle: strike up a conversation, strike up the band. A pronoun object is vanishingly rare here; speakers repeat the noun instead.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: it names the beginning of a conversation, a friendship, or a piece of music, not its continuation. They struck up a conversation in line at the post office.
entries.passive: yes, though usually without a by-phrase: a friendship was struck up between them that lasted forty years, a march was struck up and everyone stood.
entries.see also: strike on, speak to

entries.meaning: Direct profanity at someone or something.
examples: He swore at the umpire and got thrown out.
She swore at the printer for a solid minute.
Don't swear at your brother.
Somebody swore at us from a passing car.
He never swears at people, only at objects.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: swear at the umpire, swear at him. ✗ swear him at.
entries.register: everyday — the verb itself is neutral; the words it describes are the vulgar part
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity that can go on: she swore at the printer for a solid minute, he's swearing at the umpire again.
entries.passive: yes — one of the prepositional verbs that passivizes cleanly, especially with get and in the -ing form: the umpire was sworn at from the stands, nobody likes getting sworn at.
entries.see also: swear by, swear off, swear to

entries.meaning: Have complete faith in a remedy or a method — or take an oath on something sacred.
examples: My grandmother swore by cod liver oil.
He swears by that brand of tires.
Half the crew swears by it.
He swore by everything he had that he was home that night.
She swore by all she held holy.

senses.head: Have complete faith in something
body: The everyday sense, and always about something that works for the speaker whether or not it works at all. (свято верить в)
examples: My grandmother swore by cod liver oil.
He swears by that brand of tires.
Half the crew swears by it.

senses.head: Take an oath on something
body: Older and more formal: you name the thing you would forfeit if you were lying. (клясться чем-л.)
examples: He swore by everything he had that he was home that night.
She swore by all she held holy.

entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: swear by that remedy, swear by it. ✗ swear it by.
entries.verb type: stative in the everyday faith sense — a settled belief, not an act: my grandmother swore by cod liver oil, ✗ she is swearing by cod liver oil. The older oath sense is action — dynamic: he swore by everything he had that he was home that night.
entries.passive: no. Stative and prepositional at once: ✗ cod liver oil was sworn by by my grandmother, ✗ that brand of tires is sworn by. Say she swore by it or she trusted it completely.
entries.see also: swear to, swear off, stick to

entries.meaning: Put someone under oath as they take office or before they give evidence.
examples: The mayor was sworn in on Monday morning.
They swore in forty new citizens at the courthouse.
The clerk swore her in before a word of testimony.
The judge swore the witnesses in one at a time.
He gets sworn in at noon.
Two witnesses were sworn in and then sent back out into the hall.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
