entries.separable: yes — swear in the new citizens or swear the new citizens in; with a pronoun it must split: swear her in. The whole phrase is usually passive: was sworn in.
entries.register: everyday — the standard American word for taking office
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual, a ceremonial act performed on someone: the clerk swore her in before a word of testimony.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the commoner form: the mayor was sworn in on Monday morning, two witnesses were sworn in and then sent back out into the hall. Get works too: he gets sworn in at noon.
entries.see also: swear to, swear by, stand down

entries.meaning: Give something up and promise yourself you are finished with it.
examples: He swore off cigarettes in January.
She's sworn off dating coworkers.
I swore off it after the first hangover.
They swore off cable and never went back.
Every February somebody in that office swears off sugar.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: no in practice — what you renounce follows the particle, pronouns included: swear off sugar, I've sworn off it. ✗ swear it off.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — a noun or an -ing form
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual: the moment of renouncing, not the abstaining that follows. He swore off cigarettes in January; the perfect carries the result: she's sworn off dating coworkers.
entries.passive: no. The thing renounced will not become subject: ✗ cigarettes were sworn off by him, ✗ sugar is sworn off every February. Keep it active, or say he gave up cigarettes.
entries.see also: swear by, stick to

entries.meaning: State that something is true and take responsibility for it; commonest in the hedge I couldn't swear to it.
examples: I couldn't swear to the exact time.
She swore to it in court.
He'd swear to anything for the right money.
I think it was a Tuesday, but don't make me swear to it.
Nobody would swear to having seen him there.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the object follows the preposition: swear to the time, swear to it. ✗ swear it to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of vouching; most often under a modal in the hedge I couldn't swear to it, where it names an ability rather than an event.
entries.passive: restricted. Alive only in legal boilerplate — subscribed and sworn to before me this day, the affidavit was sworn to in open court. Outside that, no: ✗ the exact time couldn't be sworn to.
entries.see also: swear by, swear in, shake on

entries.meaning: Dismiss an objection or an obstacle without giving it a hearing.
examples: He swept aside every objection anyone raised.
She swept the question aside and kept talking.
They swept it aside as a detail.
The judge swept aside the procedural arguments.
You can't just sweep the whole thing aside.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.separable: yes — sweep aside the objections or sweep the objections aside; with a pronoun it must split: swept it aside.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and dismissive: a single motion, literal or figurative. He swept aside every objection anyone raised.
entries.passive: yes and natural: the procedural arguments were swept aside, the question was swept aside and she kept talking.
entries.see also: sweep away, shoot down, shut out

entries.meaning: Carry something off and destroy it, abolish it wholesale, or — in the passive — overwhelm someone with feeling.
examples: The flood swept away the bridge.
A wave swept it away in seconds.
The new law swept away sixty years of rules.
They swept the old system away in a single season.
She was swept away by the whole thing and agreed on the spot.

senses.head: Carry off and destroy
body: Water, wind, and landslides do this literally. (смыть, снести)
examples: The flood swept away the bridge.
A wave swept it away in seconds.

senses.head: Abolish completely
body: Of rules, systems, and traditions: nothing is left standing. (смести, покончить с)
examples: The new law swept away sixty years of rules.
They swept the old system away in a single season.

senses.head: be swept away — be overwhelmed by feeling
body: Passive only. (быть захваченным, потерять голову)
examples: She was swept away by the whole thing and agreed on the spot.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: смыть, снести; смести, покончить с; захлестнуть (о чувстве)
entries.separable: yes — sweep away the old rules or sweep the old rules away; with a pronoun it must split: swept it away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — the physical carrying off (the flood swept away the bridge), the wholesale abolishing (the new law swept away sixty years of rules), and the overwhelming by feeling.
entries.passive: yes, and the third sense exists in the passive only: the bridge was swept away by the flood, the old system was swept away in a single season, she was swept away by the whole thing and agreed on the spot.
entries.see also: sweep aside, sweep up, shut down

entries.meaning: Clean up by sweeping, gather things together fast, or — in the passive — get caught up in something bigger.
examples: Sweep up the glass before somebody steps in it.
He swept the shop up after closing.
You go ahead — I'll sweep up.
The papers were still spread across the table; she swept them up and left without a word.
They got swept up in the excitement and bought two.

senses.head: Clean by sweeping
body: With or without an object; sweep up on its own means do the sweeping. (подмести, замести)
examples: Sweep up the glass before somebody steps in it.
He swept the shop up after closing.
You go ahead — I'll sweep up.

senses.head: Gather things quickly
body: One armful, one motion. (собрать, сгрести)
examples: The papers were still spread across the table; she swept them up and left without a word.

senses.head: be swept up in — be caught up in something
body: Passive, of excitement, a movement, a scandal. (быть втянутым, захваченным)
examples: They got swept up in the excitement and bought two.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, and that is what welds the two words into one
entries.русский: подмести, замести; собрать, сгрести; быть втянутым (be swept up in)
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — sweep up the glass or sweep the glass up, and a pronoun splits it: sweep them up. It also works with no object: I'll sweep up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: cleaning (he swept the shop up after closing), gathering fast (she swept the papers up and left), or being caught up in something bigger.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses, and the third is passive-only: the glass was swept up before anybody stepped in it, they got swept up in the excitement and bought two. No passive from the objectless use: ✗ it was swept up by me for I'll sweep up.
entries.see also: sweep away, sweep aside, shake out

entries.meaning: Try to hit someone or something — with a fist, a bat, or a club.
examples: He swung at me and missed by a foot.
She swung at the first pitch.
Don't swing at everything they throw you.
Somebody swung at the piñata and hit the fence post.
He swung at it twice and gave up.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the target follows the preposition: swing at the ball, swing at him. ✗ swing him at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual — an attempt, not a hit: he swung at me and missed by a foot, she swung at the first pitch.
entries.passive: restricted. Possible with a human object in casual speech — I've been swung at plenty of times — but flat with a thing: ✗ the first pitch was swung at by her, ✗ the piñata was swung at.
entries.see also: swing by, strike back, set upon

entries.meaning: Stop somewhere briefly on your way to somewhere else.
examples: I'll swing by the store on the way home.
Swing by around six and we'll eat.
She swung by the office to drop off the keys.
Can you swing by and pick me up?
We swung by his place, but nobody was home.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb keeps the stress here and the preposition is reduced
entries.separable: no — the place follows the preposition: swing by the store, swing by there. ✗ swing the store by. It also works with no object at all: swing by around six.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a brief detour on the way somewhere else; American and informal. I'll swing by the store on the way home, swing by around six.
entries.passive: no. The place after by is a destination, not a promotable object: ✗ the store was swung by on the way home, ✗ the office was swung by to drop off the keys.
entries.see also: swing at, stick around
